const jwt = require("jsonwebtoken");
const { promisify } = require("util");
const bcrypt = require("bcryptjs");
// Custom Imports
const AppError = require("../utils/appError");
const catchAsync = require("../utils/catchAsync");
const User = require("../models/userModel");
const Listing = require("../models/listingModel");

const signToken = (id) => {
  return jwt.sign({ id }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, {
    expiresIn: process.env.JWT_EXPIRES_IN,
  });
};

const createSendToken = (user, statusCode, res) => {
  const token = signToken(user._id);

// Remove password from output
  user.password = undefined;

res.status(statusCode).json({
    status: "success",
    token,
    data: {
      user,
    },
  });
};

exports.signup = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
  const { username, email, password, role } = req.body;

const newUser = await User.create({
    username,
    email,
    password,
    // Allow selecting landlord vs tenant at signup (defaults to tenant)
    ...(role ? { role } : {}),
  });

createSendToken(newUser, 201, res);
});

exports.login = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
  const { email, password } = req.body;

// 1) Check if email and password exist
  if (!email || !password) {
    return next(new AppError("Please provide email and password", 400));
  }

// 2) Check if user exists
  const user = await User.findOne({ email });
  if (!user) return next(new AppError("User not found", 404));

// 3) Check if password is correct
  const correct = await user.correctPassword(password, user.password);
  if (!correct) {
    return next(new AppError("Incorrect password", 401));
  }

// 4) If everything ok, send token to client
  createSendToken(user, 200, res);
});

exports.getUser = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
  const listing = await Listing.findById(req.params.id);
  const user = await User.findById(listing.user);
  if (!user) {
    return next(new AppError("No user found with that ID", 404));
  }

user.password = undefined;

res.status(200).json({
    status: "success",
    data: user,
  });
});

exports.update = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
  const { username, email, password, avatar } = req.body.payload;

// 1) Check if user exists
  const user = await User.findById(req.params.id);
  if (!user) {
    return next(new AppError("No user found with that ID", 404));
  }

// 2) hash password
  const hashedPassword = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12);

// 3) Update user
  const newUser = await User.findByIdAndUpdate(
    req.params.id,
    {
      username,
      email,
      password: hashedPassword,
      avatar,
    },
    {
      new: true,
      runValidators: true,
    }
  );

// 4) If everything ok, send token to client
  createSendToken(newUser, 200, res);
});

exports.delete = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
  // 1) Find User
  const user = await User.findById(req.params.id);
  if (!user) {
    return next(new AppError("No user found with that ID", 404));
  }
  // 2) Delete User
  await User.findByIdAndDelete(req.params.id);

// 3) If everything ok, send token to client
  res.status(204).json({
    status: "success",
    data: null,
  });
});

exports.google = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
  const { name, email, photo } = req.body;

const user = await User.findOne({ email });

if (user) {
    // just return the user
    createSendToken(user, 200, res);
  } else {
    const password = await bcrypt.hash(Math.random().toString(), 12);

const newUser = await User.create({
  username: name,
  email,
  password,
  avatar: photo,
});

createSendToken(newUser, 201, res);

}
});

exports.protect = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
  // 1) Getting token and check of it's there
  let token;
  if (
    req.headers.authorization &&
    req.headers.authorization.startsWith("Bearer")
  ) {
    token = req.headers.authorization.split(" ")[1];
  }

if (!token) {
    return next(
      new AppError("You are not logged in! Please log in to get access.", 401)
    );
  }

// 2) Verification token
  const decode = await promisify(jwt.verify)(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET);

// 3) Check if user still exists
  const freshUser = await User.findById(decode.id);
  if (!freshUser) {
    return next(
      new AppError(
        "The user belonging to this token does no longer exist.",
        401
      )
    );
  }

  req.user = freshUser;
  next();
});
exports.requireRole = (role) => {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    if (!req.user || req.user.role !== role) {
      return res.status(403).json({
        success: false,
        message: "Access denied",
      });
    }
    next();
  };
};

exports.requirePremium = (req, res, next) => {
  if (!req.user || !req.user.premiumStatus) {
    return next(
      new AppError("Premium feature. Please upgrade your account.", 402)
    );
  }
  next();
};

1) First fix: STOP running in “Production” locally

Two problems:

The value has a capital P and a space. Your code checks process.env.NODE_ENV === "development" so it will never match.

More importantly: some tooling / error output behaves differently.

NODE_ENV=development

2) Add a try/catch around the create to force an error response

Right now, if it throws in an async handler without catchAsync, you can still get hanging.

Temporarily set signup to this:

exports.signup = async (req, res) => {
  try {
    console.log("➡️ signup hit");
    console.log("BODY:", req.body);

    const user = await User.create(req.body);

    console.log("✅ user created:", user._id);

    res.status(201).json({ status: "success", data: { user } });
  } catch (err) {
    console.error("❌ signup error:", err);
    res.status(500).json({ status: "error", message: err.message });
  }
};

Now it cannot hang silently. It will either succeed or return JSON error.

Restart server and hit Postman again.

3) The MOST likely cause: your user schema password hashing hook is broken or slow

In your earlier userModel snippet, I saw:

password: {
  minlength: 8,
  // select: false,
},

If you have a pre("save") hook like:

userSchema.pre("save", async function(next) {
  this.password = await bcrypt.hash(this.password, 12);
  next();
});

If that hook is missing next() or has a condition wrong, it can stall the save.

Quick check in server/models/userModel.js

Look for userSchema.pre("save"... and verify:

It calls next() in all paths

It has if (!this.isModified("password")) return next();

Correct version:

userSchema.pre("save", async function (next) {
  if (!this.isModified("password")) return next();
  this.password = await bcrypt.hash(this.password, 12);
  next();
});

If your hook doesn’t have that return next() or forgets next() → User.create() can hang.

Add a DB name:

This won’t usually cause a hang, but it avoids weird defaults and permission mismatches.

## Response:
1/21/2026, 11:12:17 PM

Perfect — that curl dump tells me exactly what’s going on.

What it proves

Your frontend is making a cross-site request:

Origin: http://localhost:3000

API host: http://127.0.0.1:5000

Even though both are “your machine”, the browser treats localhost and 127.0.0.1 as different sites. That’s why DevTools shows Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site.

So you’ve got a CORS / cross-origin situation and you’re likely getting occasional “network” failures from the browser when the API doesn’t answer cleanly to preflight/headers.

Fix it properly (pick ONE of these and the forever-loading dies)

Option A (best): Use CRA proxy so requests are same-origin

This avoids CORS entirely.

In client/package.json add:

"proxy": "http://localhost:5000"

In your RTK Query / axios base URL, use a relative API path:

baseUrl: "/api/v1" (NOT http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1)

Restart the client (npm start).

✅ Result: browser calls localhost:3000/api/v1/... and CRA proxies to localhost:5000.

Option B: Keep cross-origin, but FIX CORS on the backend

If you want to keep 3000 → 5000 directly, do this in your Express server:

Install CORS:

cd server
npm i cors

In server/index.js (or app.js) add before routes:

import cors from "cors";

app.use(cors({
  origin: ["http://localhost:3000", "http://127.0.0.1:3000"],
  credentials: true,
  methods: ["GET","POST","PUT","PATCH","DELETE","OPTIONS"],
  allowedHeaders: ["Content-Type","Authorization"],
}));

app.options("*", cors());

✅ Result: browser stops blocking / failing the requests.

Option C (quickest): Stop using 127.0.0.1 — use localhost everywhere

If your frontend base URL is http://127.0.0.1:5000, change it to:

http://localhost:5000

And make sure your backend is also binding to localhost normally.

✅ Result: still cross-origin (port differs) but at least host matches and you avoid some weirdness with “site” comparisons.

One more thing: your UI must not hang forever

Even with CORS fixed, if the API ever fails, your page shouldn’t be stuck behind DotLoader.

On the landing page, don’t do:

if (isLoading) return <DotLoader />

Do:

{isLoading && <DotLoader />}
{isError && <RetryBlock onRetry={refetch} />}
<Section data={data ?? []} />

So failure shows an error state, not infinite loading.

What I want you to do right now (fastest win)

Do Option A (proxy). It’s the cleanest and avoids CORS headaches completely.

If you tell me whether your client is CRA/Vite/Next, I’ll tell you the exact proxy equivalent (they differ).

const UserSchema = new mongoose.Schema(

      type: String,
      required: true,
      trim: true,
    },

    email: {

      lowercase: true,
      trim: true,

    passwordHash: {

      required: true,
    },

    phone: {
      type: String,
    },

    premium: {
      type: Boolean,
      default: false,
    },

    premiumActivatedAt: {
      type: Date,
    },
  },
  {

  }
);

// Indexes
UserSchema.index({ email: 1 }, { unique: true });
UserSchema.index({ role: 1 });
UserSchema.index({ premium: 1 });

export default mongoose.model("User", UserSchema);

  // Only hash the password if it is new or has been modified
  if (!this.isModified("password")) return next();

if (Array.isArray(room?.images) && room.images.length > 0) {
  const firstImage = room.images[0];
  return typeof firstImage === "string"
    ? firstImage
    : firstImage?.url || FALLBACK_IMAGE;
}

if (typeof room?.image === "string") return room.image;
if (typeof room?.coverImage === "string") return room.coverImage;

return FALLBACK_IMAGE;
```

So the card only knows about:

* `room.images`
* `room.image`
* `room.coverImage`

But the backend has **two separate image systems**:

* `AccommodationImage`
* `RoomImage`

The Prisma schema explicitly makes `Room.images` a relation to `RoomImage`, while `Accommodation.images` is a separate relation to `AccommodationImage`.

### More importantly: the public room API transforms the images

The backend's `decoratePublicRoom()` does this:

```js
images: (room.images || []).map((image) => image.url).filter(Boolean),
coverImage: room.images?.[0]?.url || null,
```

So **when you hit `GET /rooms/:id`**, the expected result is:

```json
{
  "images": [
    "https://..."
  ],
  "coverImage": "https://..."
}
```

not:

```json
{
  "images": [
    {
      "id": "...",
      "url": "https://..."
    }
  ]
}
```

The backend is deliberately flattening `RoomImage` objects to URL strings for the public room response.

### The likely actual failure

The upload endpoint itself is correctly storing a room image:

```js
exports.addRoomImage = ...
```

and creates:

```js
{
  roomId,
  url,
  altText,
  isCover,
  sortOrder
}
```

in `RoomImage`.

So if the user uploads an image successfully, the database can contain it.

The issue is likely **the endpoint supplying the collection of rooms to the page containing `StayCard` is not returning those `RoomImage` records in the shape that `StayCard` expects**.

That's why this is important:

> If `room.images` is absent/empty at the point where `StayCard` renders, your code has no choice but to return `FALLBACK_IMAGE`.

The fallback isn't detecting a broken image. It's detecting **missing image data**.

### There is also an architectural clue

The backend has:

```text
Accommodation
 ├── images → AccommodationImage
 └── rooms
       └── images → RoomImage
```

But your card represents a **room/stay**, not an accommodation.

Therefore, the correct image priority should be something like:

```text
room.images
↓
room.coverImage
↓
room.accommodation.images
↓
room.accommodation.coverImage
↓
fallback
```

Right now your card never checks `room.accommodation.images`.

That is a significant gap because the backend's accommodation API explicitly returns accommodation images, while the room API has its own room images.

### So I would fix it in two places

**1. Make `StayCard` resilient to both room and accommodation images.**

Something along these lines:

```ts
const getRoomImage = (room: any) => {
  const roomImages = room?.images;

  if (Array.isArray(roomImages) && roomImages.length > 0) {
    const first = roomImages[0];

    if (typeof first === "string" && first.trim()) {
      return first;
    }

    if (first?.url) {
      return first.url;
    }
  }

  if (typeof room?.coverImage === "string" && room.coverImage.trim()) {
    return room.coverImage;
  }

  const accommodationImages = room?.accommodation?.images;

  if (Array.isArray(accommodationImages) && accommodationImages.length > 0) {
    const first = accommodationImages[0];

    if (typeof first === "string" && first.trim()) {
      return first;
    }

    if (first?.url) {
      return first.url;
    }
  }

  if (
    typeof room?.accommodation?.coverImage === "string" &&
    room.accommodation.coverImage.trim()
  ) {
    return room.accommodation.coverImage;
  }

  if (typeof room?.image === "string" && room.image.trim()) {
    return room.image;
  }

  return FALLBACK_IMAGE;
};
```

**2. More importantly, fix the API feeding the StayCard.**

I would **not** rely on the card to compensate for an incomplete API response.

The public temporary-stay listing endpoint should return every room with at least:

```json
{
  "images": ["https://..."],
  "coverImage": "https://..."
}
```

for the room itself.

The backend already has the correct transformation logic in `decoratePublicRoom()`.

So the next thing I would trace is:

```text
Upload image
    ↓
RoomImage
    ↓
room listing/search endpoint
    ↓
Redux/API response
    ↓
StayCard.room
    ↓
getRoomImage()
```

**I strongly suspect the break is between `RoomImage` and the endpoint that populates the StayCard**, rather than the upload itself.

One other important point: the repo's current `main` branch does **not appear to contain the exact `StayCard` you pasted**—the repository metadata is current through August 18, while your pasted component appears to be from a newer/local frontend state. So I would not blindly modify the GitHub `main` card based only on this snippet.

You're right. I checked the repository directly, and we have the actual cause.

### The bug is in the `/stays` backend query

`StayCard` is not the main problem.

In `stayController.js`, the `/stays` search uses `getRoomSearchSelect()`. It currently asks Prisma for:

```js
images: {
  where: { isCover: true },
  orderBy: { sortOrder: "asc" },
  take: 1,
  select: {
    url: true,
  },
},
```

So the `/stays` endpoint **only receives a `RoomImage` if `isCover === true`**. 

Then `decorateStay()` does:

```js
images: selectedImages.map((image) => image.url).filter(Boolean),
coverImage: selectedImages[0]?.url || null,
```

which is otherwise correct. 

The upload endpoint, however, creates the image with:

```js
isCover: Boolean(req.body.isCover)
```

So if the upload flow doesn't explicitly send `isCover: true`, the image is stored successfully but **the `/stays` query deliberately excludes it**. 

That's exactly consistent with your symptom: **every StayCard gets the fallback even though images exist in `RoomImage`.**

### Correct fix

The search endpoint should not depend on `isCover` to determine whether a room has an image.

It should retrieve the first room image by `sortOrder`, regardless of `isCover`.

I recommend changing:

```js
images: {
  where: { isCover: true },
  orderBy: { sortOrder: "asc" },
  take: 1,
  select: {
    url: true,
  },
},
```

to:

```js
images: {
  orderBy: [
    { isCover: "desc" },
    { sortOrder: "asc" },
  ],
  take: 1,
  select: {
    url: true,
  },
},
```

That gives the search endpoint:

1. Explicit cover image first.
2. Otherwise the first uploaded image.
3. `StayCard` receives the URL either way.

The public room endpoint already retrieves **all** room images without the `isCover` restriction, confirming that this restriction is specific to the search implementation. 

### One paste block

Since you want efficiency, run this directly in `~/Creapy`:

```bash
cd ~/Creapy && python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("backend/controllers/stayController.js")
s = p.read_text()

old = '''  images: {
    where: { isCover: true },
    orderBy: { sortOrder: "asc" },
    take: 1,
    select: {
      url: true,
    },
  },'''

new = '''  images: {
    orderBy: [
      { isCover: "desc" },
      { sortOrder: "asc" },
    ],
    take: 1,
    select: {
      url: true,
    },
  },'''

if old not in s:
    raise SystemExit("ERROR: expected image query block not found")

p.write_text(s.replace(old, new, 1))
print("Fixed /stays room image selection")
PY

git diff -- backend/controllers/stayController.js && \
git add backend/controllers/stayController.js && \
git commit -m "fix: include room images in stay search results" && \
git push origin main
```

This addresses the backend defect that the `StayCard` change could not fix.

## Response:
8/18/2026, 10:33:54 AM

> **Inspected mobile headers, protected routes, login roles, and dashboard routing**
>
> 
>
> Worked for 14s

Yes. This is the correct repository, and I inspected the current `main` branch directly.

The issue is now **confirmed**, and it is more specific than the earlier investigation suggested.

### Actual root cause

The desktop and mobile Dashboard handlers are currently **different**.

The **desktop** handler already supports all four relevant roles:

- `landlord` → `/dashboard/landlord`
- `tenant` → `/dashboard/tenant`
- `provider` → `/dashboard/provider`
- `admin` / `super_admin` → `/dashboard/admin`

The current desktop code contains those routes. 

But the **mobile** handler is still the old implementation:

```text
landlord → /dashboard/landlord
tenant   → /dashboard/tenant
admin    → /dashboard/admin
anything else → /
```

So specifically, the mobile code has:

```text
else {
  navigate("/");
}
```

and **does not handle `provider` or `super_admin`**. 

That exactly explains your symptom:

> Desktop → dashboard works  
> Mobile → Dashboard sends you to `/`

### Why `/dashboard/provider` itself is not the problem

The application absolutely has a provider dashboard route:

```text
/dashboard/provider
```

and it is protected for `provider`. 

`ProtectedRoutes` also explicitly knows how to route a `provider` to `/dashboard/provider`, and handles `super_admin` as an admin. 

So the routing infrastructure is already configured correctly.

### The exact bug

It's this mobile block in:

`frontend/src/components/Header/index.tsx`

The current mobile code:

```tsx
if (userRole === "landlord") {
  navigate("/dashboard/landlord");
} else if (userRole === "tenant") {
  navigate("/dashboard/tenant");
} else if (userRole === "admin") {
  navigate("/dashboard/admin");
} else {
  navigate("/");
}
```

The desktop version immediately above it has already been updated to include `provider` and `super_admin`, which is why the behavior differs between desktop and mobile. 

### Correct fix

The best fix is **not** simply adding another `else if` to the mobile code.

The cleaner solution is to create **one `handleDashboardNavigation()` function** and have both desktop and mobile use it.

That prevents the two implementations from drifting apart again.

The function should effectively be:

```tsx
const handleDashboardNavigation = () => {
  if (userRole === "landlord") {
    navigate("/dashboard/landlord");
  } else if (userRole === "tenant") {
    navigate("/dashboard/tenant");
  } else if (userRole === "provider") {
    navigate("/dashboard/provider");
  } else if (userRole === "admin" || userRole === "super_admin") {
    navigate("/dashboard/admin");
  } else {
    navigate("/");
  }
};
```

Then desktop:

```tsx
onClick={handleDashboardNavigation}
```

And mobile:

```tsx
onClick={() => {
  handleDashboardNavigation();
  setMobileOpen(false);
}}
```

This repository therefore confirms that **the mobile-specific Dashboard handler is the immediate cause of the `/` redirect**.

I would fix `Header/index.tsx` first. There is no need to change `ProtectedRoutes` or the dashboard routes for this particular bug.

## Prompt:

## Response:
8/17/2026, 3:46:19 PM

Yes. Since production is already functional and you've cloned it, the safest approach is to turn the clone into a separate staging environment, not modify production itself.

For Town Ruins, I’d structure it like:

PRODUCTION
app.townruins.com
api.townruins.com
    ↓
production database
production storage
production secrets

STAGING
staging.townruins.com
staging-api.townruins.com
    ↓
staging database
staging storage
staging secrets

Recommended order

Clone the production codebase — already done.

Create a separate Git branch, e.g. staging.

Give staging its own environment variables/secrets.
Different DATABASE_URL

Different JWT_SECRET

Different SMTP credentials/config if appropriate

Different S3/storage bucket

Different frontend API URL

Create a separate staging PostgreSQL database.
Do not point staging at the production database.

Create separate staging storage.
Ideally something like townruins-staging rather than sharing production uploads.

Deploy the cloned application with staging-specific Docker Compose configuration.

Create staging DNS records, for example:
staging.townruins.com

staging-api.townruins.com

Configure Nginx so those domains route to the staging containers.

Run Prisma migrations against the staging DB.

Seed staging data with test accounts rather than copying sensitive production users.

Test the complete application before making changes to the staging branch.

One important decision

If your cloned environment is going onto the same Ubuntu server, we need to make sure staging does not collide with production on:

Docker container names

ports

volumes

database

Nginx server blocks

environment files

uploaded files

cron/background workers

For example:

Production:
frontend → 3000
backend  → 5000
postgres → production DB

Staging:
frontend → 3001
backend  → 5001
postgres → staging DB

Nginx can then expose both through normal HTTPS domains, so you don't need users to access :3001 or :5001.

I would not copy the production .env wholesale. Copy the structure, then explicitly replace the database, secrets, storage, URLs, and any production-only integrations.

Since you've uploaded the cloned project ZIP, I can also inspect its Docker/Compose/Nginx/env structure and tell you exactly what needs to change to make this clone staging, without changing the scope beyond that.

## Response:
8/17/2026, 3:50:52 PM

Yes - I see what you started doing. The direction is right, but I would stop before continuing, because there are a few inconsistencies that will prevent the duplicate from becoming a clean staging environment.

What you changed correctly

You are separating staging from production by changing:

Backend port 5000 → 5500

Backend Docker EXPOSE

Backend server fallback port

Docker healthcheck

E2E port

PostgreSQL database name

Docker service names

That's the right general idea.

But there are 3 problems

1. Nginx is inconsistent

You changed the Docker Compose service from:

backend:

to:

backP:

but default.conf still has:

upstream backend {
    server backend:5500;
}

That will fail because Docker DNS will now know the service as backP, not backend.

It should be:

upstream backend {
    server backP:5500;
}

However, I wouldn't rename the service at all.

You don't actually need to change:

backend:
frontend:

Service names are isolated by the Compose project/network. You can run staging with a different Compose project name, so production can still have a backend service and staging can also have a backend service.

That's much cleaner.

2. Changing the frontend container's internal port is unnecessary

You changed:

frontend:

to:

frontP:

and:

expose:
  - "80"

to:

expose:
  - "880"

But your frontend Dockerfile/nginx is almost certainly listening on port 80 internally.

expose: 880 does not magically make nginx listen on 880.

So I would leave the frontend at port 80.

You only need to separate ports that are exposed on the host. If staging and production use separate Compose projects, they can both have:

frontend → port 80 internally
backend  → port 5000 internally

and Nginx routes to the correct containers.

3. Most importantly: don't change the application backend port just to separate environments

This:

-const port = process.env.PORT || 5000;
+const port = process.env.PORT || 5500;

isn't necessary.

Better:

const port = process.env.PORT || 5000;

Then staging's .env can specify:

PORT=5500

while production retains:

PORT=5000

That keeps the source code identical between environments.

Same principle applies to render.yaml, .env.example, tests, etc.

Environment differences should primarily live in environment configuration, not source code.

The bigger issue: your database change

You changed:

POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-creapyP}

That's okay as a fallback, but the real staging separation should happen in the staging .env.

For example:

POSTGRES_DB=creapy_staging

and:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://.../creapy_staging

You absolutely do not want staging accidentally connecting to the production database.

Also this:

file="/backups/creapyPs-$$(date...

looks like an accidental naming change (creapyPs). I'd make the staging backup name explicitly:

creapy-staging-...

What I recommend you do now

Since you've already cloned production, don't keep modifying the source to make it different.

Instead, make the clone staging through configuration:

Production clone
      │
      ├── same application code
      │
      ├── staging .env
      │      PORT=5500
      │      DATABASE_URL=staging DB
      │      JWT_SECRET=staging secret
      │      storage=staging
      │
      ├── staging compose project
      │
      └── staging nginx/domain

Then you can have:

Production
app.townruins.com
api.townruins.com

Staging
staging.townruins.com
staging-api.townruins.com

One more thing I noticed

Your diff contains ^M on several newly edited lines:

+PORT=5500^M

That's a CRLF line-ending change, probably because the file was edited on Windows. It isn't inherently fatal, but you don't want your staging conversion producing noisy line-ending changes throughout the repository.

So don't commit this diff yet.

If you want, I can work from the uploaded real-app-frontend-main.zip and identify the exact minimum files/lines that should change for staging, rather than you continuing to manually change ports/service names one by one.

      retries: 5

  minio:
    image: minio/minio:latest
    command: server /data --console-address ":9001"

      MINIO_ROOT_USER: ${MINIO_ROOT_USER:?Set MINIO_ROOT_USER}
      MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD:?Set MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD}

      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  postgres-backup:

    depends_on:

        condition: service_healthy
    environment:

      PGPORT: "5432"

      PGUSER: ${POSTGRES_USER:?Set POSTGRES_USER}
      PGPASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS: ${POSTGRES_BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS:-14}

    command:

          sleep 86400
        done
    restart: unless-stopped

  backend:
    build: ./backend
    env_file:
      - ./backend/.env.staging
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy

      - "5500"
    environment:

      JWT_SECRET: "${JWT_SECRET:?Set JWT_SECRET}"
      JWT_EXPIRES_IN: "${JWT_EXPIRES_IN:-30d}"
      COOKIE_SECRET: "${COOKIE_SECRET:?Set COOKIE_SECRET}"
      S3_BUCKET: "${S3_BUCKET:-townruins-staging}"
      S3_REGION: "${S3_REGION:-us-east-1}"
      S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID: "${S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID:?Set S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"
      S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: "${S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY:?Set S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}"

      S3_BROWSER_FORCE_PATH_STYLE: "${S3_BROWSER_FORCE_PATH_STYLE:-true}"

      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s

  nginx:

5. Create staging Nginx config

Create:

nano docker/nginx/staging.conf

Use:

upstream staging_backend {
    server backend:5500;
}

upstream staging_frontend {
    server frontend:80;
}

upstream staging_minio {
    server minio:9000;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name staging.townruins.com;

    location /health {
        access_log off;
        return 200 'OK';
    }

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://staging_backend;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;

        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Port $server_port;

        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_buffering off;
        proxy_redirect off;
    }

    location ^~ /creapy-uploads/ {
        proxy_pass http://staging_minio;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;

        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

        proxy_buffering off;
        proxy_request_buffering off;
        proxy_redirect off;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://staging_frontend;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;

        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

        proxy_buffering off;
    }
}

Notice that this staging Nginx only binds:

127.0.0.1:8080

It does not touch production 80/443.

upstream staging_backend {
    server backend:5500;
}

upstream staging_frontend {
    server frontend:80;
}

upstream staging_minio {
    server minio:9000;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name staging.townruins.com;

    location /health {
        access_log off;
        return 200 'OK';
    }

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://staging_backend;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_buffering off;

        proxy_pass http://staging_minio;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_buffering off;
        proxy_request_buffering off;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://staging_frontend;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_buffering off;
    }
}
EOF

### 2. Inspect what the staging Compose actually requires

This is the key problem. Your current `docker-compose.staging.yml` uses `${...}` variables from the **Compose environment**, while `.env.staging` is not automatically used unless you explicitly pass `--env-file`.

Run:

```bash

  --env-file .env.staging \
  -p townruins-staging \
  -f docker-compose.staging.yml \
  config
```

If it now complains about `DATABASE_URL`, `JWT_SECRET`, `COOKIE_SECRET`, or S3 variables, that's expected. We need to populate them.

### 3. Generate the staging application secrets

Run:

```bash
cd ~/TownruinsP

JWT_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
COOKIE_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)

cat >> .env.staging <<EOF
JWT_SECRET=$JWT_SECRET
COOKIE_SECRET=$COOKIE_SECRET
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://towruins_staging:${DBPASS}@postgres:5432/towruins_staging
S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=towruins_staging

S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL=https://staging.townruins.com/creapy-uploads
PORT=5500
NODE_ENV=staging
EOF
```

If either says `NOT set`, don't run the block above yet; regenerate the passwords and update `.env.staging`.

## Response:
8/18/2026, 5:52:12 AM

Yes — the `curl 127.0.0.1:8080` issue is separate. Your compose currently exposes nginx only inside the Docker network, so host `127.0.0.1:8080` is not necessarily mapped.

The actual blocker is now clear:

- All 21 migrations report as applied.
- `NotificationJob` still does not exist.
- Therefore the migration was marked applied without actually creating the table, or the database was initialized inconsistently.
- Your `psql` checks used the host shell's `$POSTGRES_USER`/`$POSTGRES_DB`, which aren't set there, so it tried to connect as `root`. That check was invalid.
- The backend then crashes when its notification worker queries `"NotificationJob"`.

**Don't manually create the table yet.** First inspect the migration history and actual tables using the environment inside the Postgres container.

Run this **single block**:

```bash
cd ~/TownruinsP

echo "===== POSTGRES ENV ====="
docker compose --env-file .env.staging -p townruins-staging -f docker-compose.staging.yml exec postgres sh -c 'echo "USER=$POSTGRES_USER DB=$POSTGRES_DB"'

echo "===== ALL TABLES ====="
docker compose --env-file .env.staging -p townruins-staging -f docker-compose.staging.yml exec postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c "\dt"'

echo "===== NOTIFICATION TABLES ====="
docker compose --env-file .env.staging -p townruins-staging -f docker-compose.staging.yml exec postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c "SELECT schemaname, tablename FROM pg_tables WHERE tablename ILIKE '\''%notification%'\'' ORDER BY tablename;"'

echo "===== NOTIFICATIONJOB ====="
docker compose --env-file .env.staging -p townruins-staging -f docker-compose.staging.yml exec postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c '\''SELECT to_regclass('\''public."NotificationJob"'\'') AS notification_job;'\'''

echo "===== MIGRATION RECORD ====="
docker compose --env-file .env.staging -p townruins-staging -f docker-compose.staging.yml exec postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c "SELECT migration_name, finished_at FROM \"_prisma_migrations\" WHERE migration_name = '\''20260518_notification_system'\'';"'

echo "===== MIGRATION SQL HASH ====="
docker compose --env-file .env.staging -p townruins-staging -f docker-compose.staging.yml exec postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c "SELECT migration_name, applied_steps_count, rolled_back_at FROM \"_prisma_migrations\" WHERE migration_name = '\''20260518_notification_system'\'';"'
```

Paste the output. That will tell us whether the migration is falsely recorded as applied, whether the table exists under a different name/schema, and whether we should repair the migration history or apply the missing schema directly.

Run this single block:

```bash
cd ~/TownruinsP

echo "===== FIX BACKEND HEALTHCHECK ====="
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("docker-compose.staging.yml")
s = p.read_text()

old = "require('http').get('http://localhost:5500/', (res) => res.statusCode === 200 ? process.exit(0) : process.exit(1)"
new = "require('http').get('http://localhost:5500/', (res) => res.statusCode === 200 ? process.exit(0) : process.exit(1))"

if old not in s:
    raise SystemExit("Expected malformed healthcheck was not found")

p.write_text(s.replace(old, new))
PY

echo "===== VERIFY HEALTHCHECK ====="
docker compose --env-file .env.staging -p townruins-staging -f docker-compose.staging.yml config | grep -A12 -B2 'healthcheck:'

echo "===== VALIDATE COMPOSE ====="

echo "COMPOSE VALID"

echo "===== RECREATE STAGING ====="
docker compose --env-file .env.staging -p townruins-staging -f docker-compose.staging.yml up -d --force-recreate

sleep 15

Yes. For `stage.townruins.com`, the application is ready; the remaining work is DNS plus the host-level HTTPS reverse proxy.

### 1. DNS

At the DNS provider for `townruins.com`, create:

```text
Type: A
Name: stage
Value: <YOUR SERVER PUBLIC IPv4>
TTL: 300
```

Do not use the private address `172.31.40.185`; that is the server's internal AWS address.

Verify from the server:

```bash
dig +short stage.townruins.com
```

It should return the server's public IPv4 address.

### 2. Check whether host nginx is already installed/running

Run:

```bash
sudo systemctl status nginx --no-pager
sudo ss -ltnp | grep -E ':80 |:443 ' || true
```

Because Docker currently binds only:

```text
127.0.0.1:8080 -> Docker nginx:80
```

the public ports `80` and `443` are available for a host-level nginx.

### 3. Configure host nginx

Once DNS resolves to this server, create:

```bash
sudo tee /etc/nginx/sites-available/stage.townruins.com >/dev/null <<'EOF'
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;

    server_name stage.townruins.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;

        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}
EOF

sudo ln -sf \
  /etc/nginx/sites-available/stage.townruins.com \
  /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/stage.townruins.com

sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx
```

Then test:

```bash
curl -i http://stage.townruins.com/health
curl -I http://stage.townruins.com/
```

### 4. HTTPS

After HTTP works publicly, install/configure Certbot and let it configure the host nginx certificate:

```bash
sudo snap install --classic certbot
sudo ln -sf /snap/bin/certbot /usr/local/bin/certbot

sudo certbot --nginx -d stage.townruins.com
```

Certbot's current nginx instructions use `certbot --nginx` for obtaining and installing the certificate. ([Certbot](https://certbot.eff.org/instructions?os=ubuntufocal&ws=nginx&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Then verify renewal:

```bash
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
```

Certbot documents `renew --dry-run` for testing automatic renewal. ([Certbot](https://certbot.eff.org/instructions?os=ubuntufocal&ws=nginx&utm_source=chatgpt.com))

### 5. AWS firewall

Make sure the EC2 security group permits inbound:

```text
TCP 80   0.0.0.0/0
TCP 443  0.0.0.0/0
```

You **do not** need to expose `8080`, `5500`, PostgreSQL, or MinIO publicly.

The intended traffic path is:

```text
Internet

   v

   |

   v
Docker nginx
   |
   +--> frontend
   |
   +--> backend:5500
```

The Docker stack you've already built can remain unchanged.

**Before running the nginx/Certbot commands, run the `dig` and `systemctl/ss` checks above.** The DNS result and whether host nginx is already occupying ports 80/443 determine the exact next step.

Yes. The staging app is healthy; the remaining problem is TLS/routing.

`526` from Cloudflare means Cloudflare can reach `16.192.162.166:443`, but the origin certificate is invalid/untrusted for `stage.townruins.com`.

You already have production using ports 80/443, so **do not expose staging on those ports**. The clean setup is:

`stage.townruins.com → Cloudflare → production nginx :443 → staging nginx :8080`

But production nginx currently has no `stage.townruins.com` server block.

Run this single block from `~/Creapy`; it will add a staging HTTPS vhost that proxies to the staging nginx through the host's `127.0.0.1:8080`, obtain/use a certificate covering the staging hostname, then reload production nginx:

```bash
cd ~/Creapy

echo "===== CHECK CLOUDFLARE DNS TARGET ====="
dig +short stage.townruins.com

echo "===== CHECK EXISTING CERT SAN ====="
sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/letsencrypt/live/townruins.com/fullchain.pem \
  -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

echo "===== ADD STAGING VHOST ====="
sudo python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("docker/nginx/default.conf")
s = p.read_text()

marker = "# --- 1. API Subdomain (api.townruins.com) ---"

if "server_name stage.townruins.com;" in s:
    print("Staging vhost already exists")
else:
    block = r'''
# --- STAGING (stage.townruins.com) ---
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    http2 on;

    server_name stage.townruins.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/townruins.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/townruins.com/privkey.pem;

    client_max_body_size 50m;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://host.docker.internal:8080;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Port $server_port;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_buffering off;
        proxy_redirect off;
    }
}

'''
    if marker not in s:
        raise SystemExit("Could not find insertion marker")
    p.write_text(s.replace(marker, block + marker))
PY

echo "===== VERIFY HOST GATEWAY SUPPORT ====="
docker exec creapy-nginx-1 getent hosts host.docker.internal || true

echo "===== TEST PRODUCTION NGINX CONFIG ====="
docker exec creapy-nginx-1 nginx -t

echo "===== RELOAD PRODUCTION NGINX ====="
docker exec creapy-nginx-1 nginx -s reload

echo "===== TEST STAGING THROUGH PRODUCTION NGINX ====="

  https://stage.townruins.com/health

echo
echo "===== DONE ====="
```

**However, one important issue:** your existing certificate must contain `stage.townruins.com`. The `openssl` output above will tell us. If it does **not**, don't reload blindly with that certificate; we need to issue a certificate containing the staging hostname first.

Also, `host.docker.internal` may not resolve on this Linux Docker setup. If the test prints nothing for it, we can add `extra_hosts: host.docker.internal:host-gateway` to the production nginx compose configuration.

## Response:
8/18/2026, 7:41:40 AM

Good: the proxy path works locally, but two fixes remain:

1. `stage.townruins.com` is **not covered by the current Let's Encrypt cert**.
2. `host.docker.internal` doesn't resolve, so the config test failed. The curl result worked only because the old nginx config was still running.

Also, `/health` reached the staging backend and returned its normal 404, which confirms the proxy is reaching staging.

Run this **single block**. It adds the Docker host gateway, requests a certificate for `stage.townruins.com` using Certbot's webroot challenge, updates nginx, reloads it, and tests the real domain:

```bash
cd ~/Creapy

echo "===== ADD HOST GATEWAY TO PRODUCTION NGINX ====="
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("docker-compose.yml")
s = p.read_text()

if "host.docker.internal:host-gateway" not in s:
    needle = "    image: nginx:stable-alpine\n"
    replacement = needle + "    extra_hosts:\n      - \"host.docker.internal:host-gateway\"\n"
    if needle not in s:
        raise SystemExit("Could not find nginx image line")
    p.write_text(s.replace(needle, replacement, 1))
    print("Added extra_hosts")
else:
    print("extra_hosts already present")
PY

echo "===== RECREATE PRODUCTION NGINX WITH HOST GATEWAY ====="
docker compose -p creapy -f docker-compose.yml up -d --force-recreate nginx

echo "===== VERIFY HOST GATEWAY ====="
docker exec creapy-nginx-1 getent hosts host.docker.internal

echo "===== REQUEST STAGING CERTIFICATE ====="
sudo certbot certonly --webroot \
  -w /var/www/html \
  -d stage.townruins.com \
  --non-interactive \
  --agree-tos \
  --email admin@townruins.com \
  --keep-until-expiring || true

echo "===== CERTIFICATE CHECK ====="
sudo openssl x509 \
  -in /etc/letsencrypt/live/stage.townruins.com/fullchain.pem \
  -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName 2>/dev/null || true

echo "===== UPDATE STAGING CERT PATHS ====="
sudo sed -i \
  's#/etc/letsencrypt/live/townruins.com/fullchain.pem#/etc/letsencrypt/live/stage.townruins.com/fullchain.pem#g; s#/etc/letsencrypt/live/townruins.com/privkey.pem#/etc/letsencrypt/live/stage.townruins.com/privkey.pem#g' \
  docker/nginx/default.conf

echo "===== TEST NGINX ====="
docker exec creapy-nginx-1 nginx -t

echo "===== RELOAD NGINX ====="
docker exec creapy-nginx-1 nginx -s reload

echo "===== LOCAL DOMAIN TEST ====="
curl -skI --resolve stage.townruins.com:443:127.0.0.1 \
  https://stage.townruins.com/ | head -20

echo "===== PUBLIC DOMAIN TEST ====="
curl -sS -I https://stage.townruins.com/ | head -20
```

One caveat: the Certbot `--webroot -w /var/www/html` path must actually be served by the production nginx for `/.well-known/acme-challenge/`. Your current production config doesn't show that. **If Certbot fails**, paste only its output; don't make further changes yet.

## Response:
8/18/2026, 7:43:11 AM

The certificate issuance failed because Cloudflare is proxying the domain while the origin currently has no valid `stage.townruins.com` certificate. Then our config switched to a nonexistent certificate, causing the local 502.

The simplest fix is **Cloudflare Origin Certificate**, not Let's Encrypt. Cloudflare can issue an origin cert for `stage.townruins.com`, and nginx can use it. But that requires creating the certificate in the Cloudflare dashboard/API.

Before changing anything else, restore the production certificate so production remains safe, and keep staging routed through the new host gateway.

Run this one block:

```bash
cd ~/Creapy

echo "===== RESTORE PRODUCTION CERT PATHS ====="
sudo sed -i \
  's#/etc/letsencrypt/live/stage.townruins.com/fullchain.pem#/etc/letsencrypt/live/townruins.com/fullchain.pem#g; s#/etc/letsencrypt/live/stage.townruins.com/privkey.pem#/etc/letsencrypt/live/townruins.com/privkey.pem#g' \
  docker/nginx/default.conf

echo "===== TEST CURRENT ROUTING ====="

will reset fix the mismatch, db is currently empty

## Response:
8/11/2026, 4:15:53 PM

Yes. **If the database is genuinely empty and you don't need any existing data, `prisma migrate reset` is a reasonable way to fix this.**

It will:

1. Drop the database/schema.
2. Recreate it.
3. Apply all migrations from `prisma/migrations`.
4. Run your Prisma seed if one is configured.

Given your logs show `_prisma_migrations` is missing and `User.onboardingStatus` is missing, a reset should reconstruct the schema correctly **provided your migration files are correct**.

### Before resetting

Verify the database is actually the empty one you intend to destroy:

```bash
docker compose exec postgres psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c '\dt'
```

Then check your migrations:

```bash
ls -lah prisma/migrations
```

If the migration directory contains your expected migrations, reset it:

```bash
docker compose exec backend npx prisma migrate reset
```

It will ask for confirmation. If you're certain the DB is disposable, confirm.

### However, there's one important distinction

If this is your **production EC2 deployment**, I would prefer:

```bash
docker compose exec backend npx prisma migrate deploy
```

**only if** the migration history is intact.

In your case, `_prisma_migrations` appears to have been deleted, so `migrate deploy` may not be able to determine what has already been applied. Since you explicitly said the DB is empty, `migrate reset` is much cleaner.

Afterward verify:

```bash
docker compose exec backend npx prisma migrate status
```

and check the column:

```bash
docker compose exec postgres psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c '\d "User"'
```

You should see:

```text
onboardingStatus
onboardingCompletedAt
```

Then restart the backend to clear any old database connections/cached plans:

```bash
docker compose restart backend
```

If your Compose service isn't called `backend`, use:

```bash
docker compose config --services
```

and substitute the actual service name.

**One caution:** if "empty" means *the application has no user data*, but there are important PostgreSQL objects/extensions/configuration you want to preserve, don't reset until we've checked. Otherwise, for a disposable empty DB, reset is appropriate.

## Prompt:
8/11/2026, 4:16:36 PM

if i want to apply a specific migration

## Response:
8/11/2026, 4:16:27 PM

If you want to apply **one specific Prisma migration**, Prisma does not have a normal `migrate up <migration-name>` command.

The right approach depends on the state of the database.

### If the DB is empty

If you want to apply migrations **up to a specific migration**, Prisma's migration system isn't designed to stop at an arbitrary migration with `migrate deploy`. The simplest safe approach is to temporarily move/remove migrations that come after the target, then run:

```bash
docker compose exec backend npx prisma migrate deploy
```

But I would **not recommend modifying your migration directory on the server**.

### If you literally want to apply one migration manually

You can execute its `migration.sql`:

```bash
docker compose exec -T postgres psql \
  -U "$POSTGRES_USER" \
  -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  < prisma/migrations/20260811123456_add_onboarding/migration.sql
```

However, this has an important problem:

**Prisma will not automatically record that migration as applied in `_prisma_migrations`.**

So afterward Prisma may try to apply it again.

### Better approach for your situation

Since you said the DB is empty, if you have:

```text
prisma/migrations/
├── 001_initial/
├── 002_add_users/
├── 003_add_notifications/
├── 004_add_onboarding/
└── 005_something_else/
```

and you want `004_add_onboarding`, the cleanest solution is usually to create a **temporary database**, test the migration sequence there, and then reset the real empty database and apply the complete valid migration history:

```bash
docker compose exec backend npx prisma migrate reset
```

That gives Prisma a consistent `_prisma_migrations` history.

### If you need to apply a specific migration because a later migration is broken

That's a different situation. In that case, tell me the migration directory name, e.g.:

```text
prisma/migrations/20260811143000_add_onboarding/
```

and whether you want:

- **only that migration**, or
- **everything through that migration**

and I can give you the exact commands without corrupting Prisma's migration history.

```

This tells you whether you're actually on the expected branch and whether it tracks `origin/main`, etc.

### 2. Compare against the remote

First:

```bash
git fetch origin
```

Then:

```bash
git status
```

If you're supposed to be on `main`, check:

```bash
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main
```

If that produces commits, your local checkout is **behind** `origin/main`.

Also:

```bash
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD
```

If that produces commits, your local checkout has commits that aren't on `origin/main`.

If both are empty, your local `HEAD` matches `origin/main`.

### 3. Check exactly what Git contains

Run:

```bash
git ls-files prisma/schema.prisma
```

Then:

```bash
git log -5 --oneline -- prisma/schema.prisma
```

And:

```bash
git log -5 --oneline -- prisma/migrations
```

This is useful because you can see whether the onboarding changes actually exist in Git history.

### 4. Search the entire checked-out repository

Your previous `grep` only searched migrations. Now search everything:

```bash
grep -R -n \
  --exclude-dir=node_modules \
  --exclude-dir=.git \
  "onboardingStatus\|onboardingCompletedAt" .
```

This should tell us **where those fields are coming from**.

If you find them in:

```text
prisma/schema.prisma
```

but not:

```text
prisma/migrations/
```

then the repository itself has an un-migrated Prisma schema change.

If you find them only inside:

```text
node_modules/.prisma/
node_modules/@prisma/
```

that's also important: your generated Prisma client may be stale relative to the checked-out source.

### 5. Check the Prisma version

```bash
npx prisma --version
```

And inspect:

```bash
cat package.json | grep -n prisma
```

### 6. Most important: check what the running backend image actually contains

Your running container is:

```text
creapy-backend-1
```

Check its Prisma schema:

```bash
docker compose exec backend sh -c 'grep -n -A100 "model User" prisma/schema.prisma'
```

If `prisma/schema.prisma` isn't present inside the image, find where the application is installed:

```bash
docker compose exec backend sh
```

then:

```bash
find /app -path '*/prisma/schema.prisma' -o -path '*/schema.prisma' 2>/dev/null
```

This matters because **the code on your host and the code inside `creapy-backend-1` may not be the same thing**. For example, Docker may be running an image built from an older commit.

### 7. Check the image creation/rebuild situation

Run:

```bash
docker compose images
```

and:

```bash
docker inspect creapy-backend-1 --format '{{.Image}}'
```

If you recently pulled a new Git branch but didn't rebuild the image, the running backend can still be using the **old Prisma Client/schema**.

## Response:
8/11/2026, 11:10:00 PM

This confirms the root cause.

Your branch has **21 migrations**, Prisma considers all 21 applied, but the current `schema.prisma` contains two fields that **none of those migrations create**.

So the repository has a schema/migration inconsistency.

### Why Prisma says "up to date"

`prisma migrate status` compares the database against the **migration history**, not against every field currently present in `schema.prisma`.

So this:

```text
21 migrations found
Database schema is up to date!
```

means:

> "All 21 migration files have been applied."

It does **not** mean:

> "The database exactly matches schema.prisma."

That's why your database can be missing:

```text
onboardingStatus
onboardingCompletedAt
```

while Prisma reports everything as up to date.

### Your Git history confirms it

The fields were introduced in:

```text
d3a5de1 frontend: add admin onboarding RTK endpoints, claim page, bulk import UI (initial)
```

But:

```bash
git grep ... backend/prisma/migrations
```

found no migration containing them.

Therefore `d3a5de1` changed the Prisma schema without adding a migration.

---

## The correct fix

Since you said the database is empty, generate a migration from the current schema.

Do this from the `backend` directory:

```bash
cd backend
npx prisma migrate dev --name add_onboarding_fields
```

Before running it, you can preview what Prisma thinks needs to change with:

```bash
npx prisma migrate dev --name add_onboarding_fields --create-only
```

I recommend **`--create-only` first** in your situation.

It should create something like:

```text
backend/prisma/migrations/
└── 20260811xxxxxx_add_onboarding_fields/
    └── migration.sql
```

Then inspect it:

```bash
cat prisma/migrations/*_add_onboarding_fields/migration.sql
```

You should see SQL adding the two columns, approximately:

```sql
ALTER TABLE "User"
ADD COLUMN "onboardingStatus" TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'not_started',
ADD COLUMN "onboardingCompletedAt" TIMESTAMP(3);
```

If that's what you see, then apply it:

```bash
npx prisma migrate dev
```

Then verify:

```bash
npx prisma migrate status
```

and on PostgreSQL:

```bash
docker compose exec postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -c '\''\d "User"'\'''
```

You should then see:

```text
onboardingStatus
onboardingCompletedAt
```

### One important point about your branch

Because this is the `stagging` branch and you're apparently using the server itself to generate the migration, **don't forget to commit the new migration**:

```bash
git status
git add backend/prisma/migrations
git commit -m "db: add onboarding fields"
git push origin stagging
```

Otherwise the database will have the fix, but the migration won't exist in Git, and the next deployment can reproduce the problem.

If you want to be especially safe, use `--create-only` first and **paste the generated `migration.sql` here before applying it**. We can verify that Prisma is only adding the two expected columns.

## Prompt:
8/11/2026, 11:43:29 AM

i want to flip a domain how do i make it more valueable

## Response:
8/11/2026, 11:43:20 AM

Yes. The main goal is to turn the domain from **“a name I own”** into **“a name a specific buyer would pay for.”**

### 1. Start with the domain itself

The biggest factors are:

- **Short** - ideally 5-12 characters.
- **Easy to spell and pronounce**
- **.com** - generally the strongest resale extension.
- **Commercial meaning** - words connected to businesses, products, services, or industries.
- **No hyphens/numbers** unless there's a strong reason.
- **Brandable** - sounds like something a startup could actually use.
- **Clear niche** - e.g. a domain relating to AI, finance, cybersecurity, real estate, etc.

For example, a domain like `QuickLedger.com` has a clearer potential buyer than something random like `xqvtr.com`.

### 2. Don't just wait for the domain to appreciate

You can increase its attractiveness by creating a **mini brand around it**:

- Build a simple landing page.
- Create a professional logo/brand concept.
- Explain what the name could be used for.
- Put a clear **“Domain for Sale”** page on it.
- If appropriate, create a small demo or prototype showing how the domain could be used.

This doesn't necessarily make the domain intrinsically more valuable, but it can make a buyer **understand the value faster**.

### 3. Find potential buyers

This is often more important than adding features.

Suppose you own:

**`ExampleAI.com`**

Potential buyers could include:

- AI startups
- AI software companies
- agencies
- developers launching AI products
- companies already using a worse domain

Look for businesses whose current name closely matches your domain. A domain is worth much more when you can identify **10-50 plausible buyers** rather than hoping someone randomly discovers it.

### 4. Check comparable sales

Before setting a price, research what similar domains have actually sold for. Don't rely solely on automated appraisal tools.

Useful marketplaces/data sources include:

- [NameBio](https://namebio.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - historical domain sales data
- [Sedo](https://sedo.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - domain marketplace
- [Afternic](https://www.afternic.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - domain marketplace
- [GoDaddy Auctions](https://auctions.godaddy.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - domain auctions

### 5. Avoid spending money just to make it look valuable

If you're flipping domains, be careful about:

- expensive logos
- elaborate websites
- unnecessary hosting
- paid appraisal services
- buying dozens of weak domains
- trademarked names

A good domain with a strong buyer is generally much more valuable than a mediocre domain with a beautiful website.

### A simple flipping strategy

**Buy → research → improve positioning → identify buyers → list → outbound to relevant businesses → negotiate.**

If you **give me the domain you're thinking of flipping**, I can evaluate the name itself, its likely buyer types, weaknesses, and what I'd do to increase its resale potential.

## Prompt:
8/11/2026, 11:48:13 AM

what happens when the name i own is the name of another company with noo digital presence, that makes it hard to sell

## Response:
8/11/2026, 11:48:04 AM

It can actually be an interesting situation, but there is an important distinction:

### If it's the exact name of an existing company

The company may be your **most obvious potential buyer**, but you should **not assume they have to buy it** just because you own the domain.

If the company has no website or digital presence, that can mean:

- They may not realize the domain exists.
- They may not care about having a website.
- They may use a different domain already.
- They may eventually want the domain once they start expanding.
- They may have trademark rights that create legal complications for you.

### The big issue is trademarks

Before trying to sell it, check whether the company's name is a registered trademark in the relevant countries/classes.

If you registered the domain **because you knew of the company and wanted to sell the domain to them**, that's much riskier than independently registering an unused domain name and later discovering a company with that name.

Don't build a strategy around forcing the company to pay you.

### If they genuinely have no digital presence

I'd approach it differently:

1. **Research the company** — how established is it, what industry is it in, and does the name actually match your domain?
2. **Check trademarks**.
3. **Look for other potential meanings of the domain**. A generic domain can have multiple buyers.
4. **Create a clean landing page** showing that the domain is available.
5. **Identify businesses that could use the name**, rather than relying exclusively on that one company.
6. If appropriate, make a **professional, non-threatening offer** to the company.

For example, if you own `BrightStone.com` and discover a small construction company called Bright Stone Construction that has no website, the domain could potentially be valuable to them—but it might also be valuable to completely unrelated businesses.

### One thing I'd avoid

Don't contact them with something like:

> "I own your company name's domain. Pay me $5,000 or you'll never get it."

That can create unnecessary legal and negotiation problems.

Instead, treat it as a normal asset:

> "I own BrightStone.com and noticed your business operates under the Bright Stone name. If you're interested in acquiring the domain for your online presence, I'd be happy to discuss it."

If you tell me **the actual domain name and what the other company does**, I can help you assess whether you've got a potentially valuable generic domain, a company-specific domain, or a trademark risk.

```tsx

  </>
);
```

JavaScript/TypeScript does not allow two `const` declarations with the same name in the same scope.

If the two functions are duplicates, keep one:

```tsx

    ...
  </>
);
```

If they are actually two different implementations, rename one, for example:

function buildPageArray(totalPages: number, currentPage: number): PaginationItem[] {
const pages: number[] = [];
const addPage = (page: number) => {
if (page >= 1 && page <= totalPages && pages.indexOf(page) === -1) {
pages.push(page);
}
};

addPage(1);

for (let page = currentPage - 2; page <= currentPage + 2; page += 1) {
addPage(page);
}

addPage(totalPages);
pages.sort((left, right) => left - right);

const items: PaginationItem[] = [];

for (let index = 0; index < pages.length; index += 1) {
const page = pages[index];
const previousPage = index > 0 ? pages[index - 1] : null;

```
if (previousPage !== null && page - previousPage > 1) {
  items.push(previousPage === 1 ? "ellipsis-start" : "ellipsis-end");
}

items.push(page);
```

}

return items;
}

case "success":
case "verified":
return statusChipColors.success;
case "checked\_in":
case "refunded":
return statusChipColors.info;
case "pending":
case "pending\_confirmation":
case "pending\_payment":
case "unsettled":
case "warning":
return statusChipColors.warning;
case "error":
case "failed":
case "failure":
case "declined":
case "rejected":
case "cancelled":
case "canceled":
case "expired":
return statusChipColors.error;
default:
return statusChipColors.default;
}
}

function formatLocation(
value?: { province?: string; city?: string } | null
) {
return [value?.province, value?.city].filter(Boolean).join(" / ") || "—";
}

const handleConfirmRevive = async () => {
if (selectedCount === 0) {
setShowConfirm(false);
return;
}

```
try {
  const idNameMap: Record<string, string> = {};
  listings.forEach((item) => {
    idNameMap[item._id] = item.name;
  });

  const result = await bulkRevive({ ids: Object.keys(selectedIds) }).unwrap();
  const revivedCount = result.revived.length;
  const failedCount = result.failed.length;

  let message = `${revivedCount} listings revived successfully.`;

  if (failedCount > 0) {
    const failureDetails = result.failed
      .slice(0, 1)
      .map((failure: BulkReviveFailure) => {
        const label =
          idNameMap[failure.id ?? ""] || failure.id || "Unknown listing";
        return `${label} - ${failure.reason || "Unknown error"}`;
      })
      .join(", ");

    message =
      revivedCount > 0
        ? `${revivedCount} revived. ${failedCount} failed: ${failureDetails}`
        : `Revival failed. ${failureDetails}`;
  }

  setToast({
    open: true,
    message,
    type:
      revivedCount > 0 && failedCount === 0
        ? "success"
        : revivedCount > 0
        ? "warning"
        : "error",
  });
  setSelectedIds({});
  setShowConfirm(false);
  triggerSearch({ ...expiredFilters, limit: ROWS_PER_PAGE });
} catch (error) {
  setToast({
    open: true,
    message: getErrorMessage(error, "An error occurred during revival."),
    type: "error",
  });
}
```

};

const openEditLegalDialog = (doc: LegalDocument) =>
setLegalDialog({
open: true,
mode: "edit",
doc,
slug: doc.slug,
title: doc.title,
content: doc.content,
});

const closeLegalDialog = () =>
setLegalDialog({
open: false,
mode: "create",
doc: null,
slug: "",
title: "",
content: "",
});

const handleSaveLegalDoc = async () => {
try {
if (legalDialog.mode === "edit" && legalDialog.doc) {
await updateLegalDoc({
id: legalDialog.doc.id,
title: legalDialog.title,
content: legalDialog.content,
}).unwrap();
} else {
await createLegalDoc({
slug: legalDialog.slug,
title: legalDialog.title,
content: legalDialog.content,
}).unwrap();
}
setToast({ open: true, message: "Legal document saved.", type: "success" });
closeLegalDialog();
} catch (error) {
setToast({
open: true,
message: getErrorMessage(error, "Unable to save legal document."),
type: "error",
});
}
};

const handleArchiveLegalDoc = async (doc: LegalDocument) => {
if (!window\.confirm(`Archive ${doc.title}?`)) return;

    type: "error",

}

## Response:
8/10/2026, 9:33:54 AM

This is a different error, and it is now coming from your `AppSelect` component rather than `Admin.tsx`.

The key part is:

```text
TS2312: An interface can only extend an object type or intersection
of object types with statically known members.

interface AppSelectProps extends SelectProps {
                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^
```

### Why this happens

Your `AppSelect.tsx` probably has something like:

```tsx
import Select, { SelectProps } from "@mui/material/Select";

interface AppSelectProps extends SelectProps {
  label?: string;
  options: AppSelectOption[];
}
```

In the version of MUI/types you're using, `SelectProps` is a **union/generic type**, and TypeScript does not allow an interface to extend it.

### Fix

Change the interface to a type intersection.

Find:

```tsx
interface AppSelectProps extends SelectProps {
  label?: string;
  options: AppSelectOption[];
}
```

Change it to:

```tsx
type AppSelectProps = SelectProps & {
  label?: string;
  options: AppSelectOption[];
};
```

That is the direct fix for TS2312.

### Then rebuild

Use:

```bash
npm run build
```

rather than:

```bash
npm run build --no-cache
```

`--no-cache` is not a valid way to disable the relevant build cache here, which is why npm keeps reporting:

```text
npm warn invalid config cache=false
npm warn invalid config Must be valid filesystem path
```

The `fs.F_OK` message is also only a Node deprecation warning. It isn't causing the compilation failure.

### If another TypeScript error appears

That's expected when fixing a chain of compile errors. Run:

```bash
npm run build
```

and address the **first `Failed to compile` / TS error** it reports.

For this one, the exact change is:

```diff
-interface AppSelectProps extends SelectProps {
+type AppSelectProps = SelectProps & {
   label?: string;
   options: AppSelectOption[];
-}
+};
```

If you paste your `AppSelect.tsx`, I can check whether there are any related MUI/TypeScript issues in that component before you rebuild.

## Response:
8/10/2026, 9:35:16 AM

Yes. The TS2312 error is caused by this line:

```ts
interface AppSelectProps extends SelectProps {
```

Change it to a type intersection. There is also a JSX issue in the code you pasted: `{label && {label}}` should be `{label && label}`.

Here is the corrected component:

**document: **

```tsx
import {
  FormControl,
  InputLabel,
  MenuItem,
  Select,
  SelectProps,
} from "@mui/material";

interface AppSelectOption {
  label: string;
  value: string | number;
}

type AppSelectProps = SelectProps & {
  label?: string;
  options: AppSelectOption[];
};

const selectFocusSx = {
  "&.MuiInputBase-root": {
    minHeight: 48,
    borderRadius: "12px",
    backgroundColor: "background.paper",
  },
  "& .MuiOutlinedInput-notchedOutline": {
    borderColor: "divider",
  },
  "&.MuiOutlinedInput-root.Mui-focused .MuiOutlinedInput-notchedOutline": {
    borderColor: "#B8975A",
  },
};

const formControlFocusSx = {
  "& .MuiInputLabel-root.Mui-focused": {
    color: "#B8975A",
  },
};

const AppSelect = ({
  label,
  options,
  sx,
  ...props
}: AppSelectProps) => {
  const labelId = label
    ? `${props.name || "app-select"}-label`
    : undefined;

  return (
    <FormControl
      fullWidth
      size={props.size || "medium"}
      sx={formControlFocusSx}
    >
      {label && <InputLabel id={labelId}>{label}</InputLabel>}

      <Select
        labelId={labelId}
        label={label}
        sx={[
          selectFocusSx,
          ...(Array.isArray(sx) ? sx : sx ? [sx] : []),
        ]}
        {...props}
      >
        {options.map((option) => (
          <MenuItem key={`${option.value}`} value={option.value}>
            {option.label}
          </MenuItem>
        ))}
      </Select>
    </FormControl>
  );
};

export default AppSelect;
```

There are **three relevant corrections** here:

1. **TS2312 fix**
   ```ts
   type AppSelectProps = SelectProps & {
   ```
   instead of:
   ```ts
   interface AppSelectProps extends SelectProps {
   ```

2. **Label JSX**
   ```tsx
   {label && <InputLabel id={labelId}>{label}</InputLabel>}
   ```
   Your pasted `{label && {label}}` is not valid JSX for rendering the label.

3. **Safer `sx` handling**
   ```ts
   sx ? [sx] : []
   ```
   prevents an `undefined` entry from being added to the array.

One thing to watch: your `Admin.tsx` calls `AppSelect` with `size="small"` and also without a `label`, so this implementation supports both cases.

Now run:

```bash
npm run build
```

Do not add `--no-cache`. If it reports another `TS` error, fix that next error rather than changing the build command.

## Response:
8/10/2026, 10:18:15 AM

The current error is straightforward: `integration.test.ts` has no `import` or `export`, so TypeScript treats it as a global script. Your Create React App build uses `isolatedModules`, which requires this file to be a module.

### Fix

Add this as the **first or last line** of `integration.test.ts`:

```ts
export {};
```

For example:

```ts
/**
 * Integration tests for admin onboarding flows
 * Tests the complete user journey through bulk import → claim → onboarding
 */

export {};

describe('Admin Onboarding Integration Flows', () => {
  // ...
});
```

Then run:

```bash
npm run build
```

### Why this happens

Your test currently contains only:

```ts
describe(...)
test(...)
```

There are no imports/exports, so TypeScript considers it a **global script**.

Adding:

```ts
export {};
```

doesn't change the test behavior. It simply tells TypeScript:

> "Treat this file as an ES module."

That satisfies `--isolatedModules`.

### One important point

The file you pasted is also full of Markdown code fences such as:

```text
```
test(...)
```
```

If those backticks are **actually present in `integration.test.ts`**, remove them. They are not valid TypeScript.

The file should contain normal TypeScript only:

```ts
test('system validates CSV before preview', () => {
  const csvData = {
    valid: [
      {
        firstName: 'John',
        lastName: 'Doe',
        email: 'john@example.com',
        phone: '123',
        role: 'tenant',
      },
    ],
    invalid: [
      { errors: ['Invalid email'], row: 2 },
    ],
  };

  expect(csvData.valid.length).toBe(1);
  expect(csvData.invalid.length).toBe(1);
});
```

not:

```text
```
test('system validates CSV before preview', () => {
```

### Also check the filename

If this is intended to be a Jest test, I'd keep it as:

```text
integration.test.ts
```

and make sure it isn't accidentally being imported into your production application.

If `npm run build` still tries to compile test files after adding `export {}`, then the next issue is likely your TypeScript/CRA configuration, specifically whether test files are being included in the production `tsconfig`.

function buildSearchParams(params: Record\<string, string | number | undefined>) {
const searchParams = new URLSearchParams();

Object.entries(params).forEach(([key, value]) => {
if (value !== undefined && value !== null && value !== "") {
searchParams.append(key, String(value));
}
});

const queryString = searchParams.toString();
return queryString ? `?${queryString}` : "";
}

## Response:
8/10/2026, 10:22:05 AM

This error is because `"Invitation"` is being used as an RTK Query tag, but `"Invitation"` is **not included in the tag types declared in your `apiSlice`**.

Your code here is valid in isolation:

```ts
providesTags: (result) =>
  result
    ? [
        ...result.data.map((inv: any) => ({
          type: "Invitation" as const,
          id: inv.id,
        })),
        { type: "Invitation" as const, id: "LIST" },
      ]
    : [{ type: "Invitation" as const, id: "LIST" }],
```

But TypeScript is telling you that `apiSlice` only knows about tags such as:

```text
"Listing"
"Payment"
"AdminListing"
"Stay"
...
"WalletTransaction"
```

and **doesn't know `"Invitation"`**.

## Fix 1 — recommended

Open:

```text
src/store/apiSlice.ts
```

or wherever your `apiSlice` is defined.

You will likely have something similar to:

```ts
export const apiSlice = createApi({
  reducerPath: "api",
  baseQuery: ...,
  tagTypes: [
    "Listing",
    "Payment",
    "AdminListing",
    // ...
    "WalletTransaction",
  ],
  endpoints: () => ({}),
});
```

Add:

```ts
"Invitation",
```

and, based on your code, make sure `"User"` is also present.

For example:

```ts
export const apiSlice = createApi({
  reducerPath: "api",
  baseQuery,
  tagTypes: [
    "Listing",
    "Payment",
    "AdminListing",
    "Stay",
    "StayBooking",
    "Provider",
    "AdminBooking",
    "Room",
    "ProviderBooking",
    "ProviderProfile",
    "ProviderAvailability",
    "ProviderSettlement",
    "WalletTransaction",

    // Admin/onboarding tags
    "Invitation",
    "User",
    "AuditLog",
    "AdminAccommodation",
    "AdminReview",
    "Dispute",
    "Report",
  ],
  endpoints: () => ({}),
});
```

Use your **existing complete tag list** and simply add the missing names rather than replacing the list.

---

## Why this appeared now

You added:

```ts
listInvitations: builder.query<{ data: any[] }, void>({
```

with:

```ts
providesTags: (result) =>
  result
    ? [
        ...result.data.map((inv: any) => ({
          type: "Invitation" as const,
          id: inv.id,
        })),
        { type: "Invitation" as const, id: "LIST" },
      ]
    : [{ type: "Invitation" as const, id: "LIST" }],
}),
```

RTK Query's `builder` gets its allowed tag names from `apiSlice.tagTypes`.

So this:

```ts
type: "Invitation"
```

must correspond to:

```ts
tagTypes: [
  ...
  "Invitation",
]
```

Otherwise TypeScript correctly rejects it.

### You have another missing-tag issue

Your file also contains:

```ts
getAdminUsers: builder.query<...>({
  ...
  providesTags: (result) =>
    result
      ? [
          ...result.data.map((user: any) => ({
            type: "User" as const,
            id: user.id || user._id,
          })),
          { type: "User" as const, id: "LIST" },
        ]
      : [{ type: "User" as const, id: "LIST" }],
}),
```

and:

```ts
completeOnboarding: builder.mutation<any, void>({
  ...
  invalidatesTags: ["User"],
}),
```

Therefore `"User"` must also be in `tagTypes`.

You already use `"AuditLog"`, `"AdminAccommodation"`, `"AdminReview"`, `"Dispute"`, and `"Report"` throughout this file, so those also need to exist in `tagTypes`. If they already do, leave them alone.

## Then rebuild

Run:

```bash
npm run build
```

You should not need to modify this `listInvitations` code.

If you want to verify exactly which tags your `apiSlice` currently has, run:

```bash
grep -n "tagTypes" src/store/apiSlice.ts
```

If your `apiSlice.ts` is somewhere else:

```bash
grep -R "tagTypes" src --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx"
```

### One more thing

Your pasted source contains Markdown fences around some sections:

```text
```
getAdminUsers: ...
...
archiveLegalDoc: ...
```
```

If those backticks are actually in the `.ts` file, **remove them**. They will cause another syntax error after this tag error is fixed.

The immediate build failure, however, is specifically:

```text
"Invitation" is not assignable to the allowed tag types
```

So the first change is to add `"Invitation"` to `apiSlice.tagTypes`, and `"User"` as well if it isn't already there.

The error is because `userRole` is declared **inside `listingHandler`**, but you also use it inside `UploadHandler`, where it is out of scope.

You currently have:

```ts
const UploadHandler = (...) => {
  ...
  if (userRole !== "landlord") {
```

but `userRole` only exists here:

```ts
const listingHandler = async (...) => {
  ...
  const userRole = useTypedSelector(selectedUserRole);
```

There is also a second issue: **you cannot call `useTypedSelector` inside `listingHandler`** because hooks must be called at the component's top level.

### Fix

You already have:

```ts
const userId = useTypedSelector(selectedUserId);
const token = useTypedSelector(selectedUserToken);
```

Add the role alongside them:

```ts
const userId = useTypedSelector(selectedUserId);
const token = useTypedSelector(selectedUserToken);
const userRole = useTypedSelector(selectedUserRole);
```

Then **remove** this line from `listingHandler`:

```ts
const userRole = useTypedSelector(selectedUserRole);
```

So the relevant section becomes:

```ts
const CreateListing = () => {
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  const { id } = useParams();

  const userId = useTypedSelector(selectedUserId);
  const token = useTypedSelector(selectedUserToken);
  const userRole = useTypedSelector(selectedUserRole);

  const [getR2SignedUrl] = useGetR2SignedUrlMutation();
```

And your `listingHandler` should start like this:

```ts
const listingHandler = async (data: listingForm) => {
  const resolvedUserId = userId;

  if (!resolvedUserId) {
    setToast({
      ...toast,
      message: "Session expired. Please log in again.",
      appearence: true,
      type: "error",

```

Your existing `UploadHandler` can then safely use:

```ts

    appearence: true,

  });

```

### One more thing to check

Your role may be uppercase depending on how your Redux auth state is populated, for example `"LANDLORD"` rather than `"landlord"`.

If your backend stores roles as uppercase, use:

```ts

```

That is safer if the role can arrive with different casing.

So the immediate fix is:

```ts
const userId = useTypedSelector(selectedUserId);
