The solution is to stop duplicating the dashboard-routing logic between desktop and mobile.

Right now both versions have this:

if (userRole === "landlord") {
  navigate("/dashboard/landlord");
} else if (userRole === "tenant") {
  navigate("/dashboard/tenant");
} else if (userRole === "admin") {
  navigate("/dashboard/admin");
} else {
  navigate("/");
}

The problem is that provider isn't handled, even though the application has /dashboard/provider.

Fix

Create one dashboard navigation function in Header/index.tsx:

const handleDashboardNavigation = () => {
  switch (userRole) {
    case "landlord":
      navigate("/dashboard/landlord");
      break;

    case "tenant":
      navigate("/dashboard/tenant");
      break;

    case "provider":
      navigate("/dashboard/provider");
      break;

    case "admin":
    case "super_admin":
      navigate("/dashboard/admin");
      break;

    default:
      console.warn("Unknown user role:", userRole);
      navigate("/");
  }
};

Then both desktop and mobile simply call:

onClick={handleDashboardNavigation}

For mobile, keep the menu closing:

onClick={() => {
  handleDashboardNavigation();
  setMobileOpen(false);
}}

But there's one thing I'd verify before changing it

Your actual user role may not be "provider". It could be something like:

property_manager
accommodation_provider
service_provider

If that's the case, adding "provider" alone won't fix the problem.

Since you have the project ZIP uploaded, I can inspect the actual role definitions and dashboard routing across the frontend and tell you exactly what the mobile handler should be changed to, rather than guessing.

Yes. I checked the actual frontend code and the backend seed structure before recommending a change. There are several possible causes, and we should not blindly patch the mobile button yet.

What I found

1. Desktop and mobile use the same role logic

In src/components/Header/index.tsx:

Desktop Dashboard: lines 221–231

Mobile Dashboard: lines 395–405

Both do:

if (userRole === "landlord") {
  navigate("/dashboard/landlord");
} else if (userRole === "tenant") {
  navigate("/dashboard/tenant");
} else if (userRole === "admin") {
  navigate("/dashboard/admin");
} else {
  navigate("/");
}

So there is no intentional mobile-only / route.

The HTML you showed is definitely the mobile ListItemButton, but its routing logic is the same as desktop.

2. provider is a real role, and Header does NOT handle it

This is a confirmed bug.

The application has:

/dashboard/provider

and App.tsx protects it with:

allowedRoles={["provider"]}

ProtectedRoutes.tsx also explicitly knows about:

role === "provider"
  ? "/dashboard/provider"

The backend seed creates users with:

role: 'provider'

But Header completely omits provider.

Therefore:

userRole = provider
       ↓
Header Dashboard
       ↓
not landlord
not tenant
not admin
       ↓
navigate("/")

This is definitely one cause.

3. super_admin is another possible problem

Your previous environment has a super_admin user, and the auth data can contain that role.

But the Header only recognizes:

admin

not:

super_admin

So a super admin will also hit:

navigate("/");

That's another confirmed routing gap.

4. The role comes entirely from Redux/localStorage

selectedUserRole is:

state.auth?.user?.data?.user?.role

And the initial Redux user comes from:

localStorage.getItem("user")

So if the stored login object is missing or has a different structure, userRole becomes undefined.

Then the Header does:

navigate("/");

We therefore need to check the actual stored user object on the affected device.

5. There is also a broader inconsistency

Login has the same incomplete routing:

landlord → dashboard/landlord
tenant   → dashboard/tenant
admin    → dashboard/admin
anything else → /

Google OAuth has the same issue.

So even if we fix Header, the application has three separate places with duplicated dashboard-routing logic:

Header
Login
Google OAuth

That makes this kind of bug likely to recur.

What I would NOT do yet

I would not change the code yet.

First, on the mobile browser where the problem occurs, let's determine what userRole actually is.

Run this in the browser's DevTools console while logged in:

JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user") || "null")

And specifically:

JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user") || "null")?.data?.user?.role

Expected result

If it returns:

"provider"

then we have identified the exact cause.

If it returns:

"landlord"

or:

"tenant"

then the provider-role issue is not the cause, and we'll investigate why the mobile click is behaving differently.

If it returns:

undefined

then the problem is the auth/localStorage state, not the mobile button itself.

One more useful test

On the affected mobile browser, run:

console.log({
  user: JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user") || "null"),
  role: JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user") || "null")?.data?.user?.role,
  avatar: JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user") || "null")?.data?.user?.avatar,
  path: window.location.pathname
})

Send me that output. Then I can tell you which of the causes is actually responsible before we touch production/staging code.

Yes. Now that staging is reachable, I would stop treating production work as a loose list of bugs/features and turn it into a Production Readiness Program with four things running in parallel:

Map everything remaining

Break it into independently assignable work

Track it against staging → production gates

Define who watches production and who responds when something breaks

Given the Town Ruins state we've been working through, I would structure it like this.

1. First, create one master production map

Don't start by assigning random tickets yet. First classify every remaining item into these buckets:

Workstream
What goes here
P0 — Production blockers
Anything that can prevent launch or cause data/security loss
P1 — Core functionality
Login, signup, onboarding, listings, bookings, payments, notifications, etc.
P2 — Admin/operations
Admin dashboard, moderation, provider onboarding, user management
P3 — UX/polish
UI bugs, responsiveness, wording, loading states
Infrastructure
Docker, Nginx, SSL, database, MinIO/storage, backups, deployment
Security
Authentication, authorization, secrets, token handling, rate limiting
Observability
Logs, health checks, alerts, uptime monitoring
Documentation
User guides, admin procedures, incident/runbooks
Testing
E2E, regression, API tests, staging acceptance

The important part is that "feature incomplete" and "production dangerous" aren't treated equally.

2. Use staging as the production rehearsal environment

Now that staging is up, make it the place where work gets validated before it is allowed toward production.

The basic pipeline should become:

Backlog → Assigned → In Development → PR → Staging → QA → Production Ready → Production

No direct:

Developer → Production

For each item, require:

What is broken/missing?

Expected behaviour

Owner

Priority

PR

Staging test

QA result

Production status

That gives you a very clear answer to "what is actually stopping us from going live?"

3. Split work by ownership, not just by feature

Since you now have two developers, don't have both people jumping between everything.

I'd use something roughly like:

You / Technical Lead

Architecture

Production infrastructure

Deployment

Security

Database

Critical backend issues

Production incident coordination

Final production approval

Developer 2

Frontend features

Admin dashboard

User/provider flows

UI/UX bugs

Frontend regression testing

Then divide backend work into discrete tickets that can be handed over rather than keeping one giant "backend fixes" task.

The key is to avoid both developers touching the same area unnecessarily.

4. Establish a "definition of done"

A ticket isn't finished merely because the developer says it works.

For Town Ruins I'd use:

Development complete

Code implemented

Local testing completed

No known console/runtime errors

PR created

Staging complete

Merged/deployed to staging

API tested

Relevant database behaviour tested

Production ready

Production complete

Deployed

Smoke test passed

Monitoring confirms healthy

No abnormal errors after deployment

This alone will dramatically reduce the "I thought it was finished" problem.

BACKLOG
   ↓

   ↓

   ↓
CODE REVIEW

STAGING

   ↓

And use priorities:

This gives you a live answer to:

"How much is actually left before production?"

Instead of saying:

"We're 70% done."

Track:

Gate 1 — Infrastructure

Production server

Only after these gates are green should you call the system production ready.

Don't make monitoring an abstract responsibility of "the developers."

Create explicit roles.

Primary on-call

Responsible for:

First response to alerts

Checking production health

Investigating incidents

Determines business impact:

Can users continue using Town Ruins?

They don't need to debug Docker—they determine operational priority.

For a two-person development team, one person can hold multiple roles, but the responsibilities should still be explicitly documented.

8. Define incident severity now

For example:

SEV-1 — Critical

Entire application unavailable, major data loss/corruption, serious security incident.

Response: immediate.

SEV-2 — Major

Major feature unavailable or significant percentage of users affected.

Response: urgent.

SEV-3 — Normal

Limited functionality broken with workaround.

Response: normal development queue.

SEV-4 — Minor

UI issue, cosmetic bug, low-impact defect.

Response: backlog.

This prevents someone waking everybody up at 2 AM because a button is misaligned.

9. Speed comes from removing dependencies

This is probably the biggest opportunity for you now.

Don't make the entire remaining project one giant sequence.

For example:

┌── Frontend ────────┐

Several streams can progress simultaneously.

The rule should be:

Only block a task when there is a real dependency.

For example, frontend doesn't need to wait for the entire backend to be "finished." It can work against the existing staging API/mock boundary while specific backend endpoints are being completed.

PRODUCTION

api.townruins.com

production storage
production secrets

STAGING
staging.townruins.com
staging-api.townruins.com
    ↓
staging database
staging storage
staging secrets

Recommended order

Clone the production codebase — already done.

Create a separate Git branch, e.g. staging.

Give staging its own environment variables/secrets.
Different DATABASE_URL

Different JWT_SECRET

Different SMTP credentials/config if appropriate

Different S3/storage bucket

Different frontend API URL

Do not point staging at the production database.

Create staging DNS records, for example:
staging.townruins.com

staging-api.townruins.com

Run Prisma migrations against the staging DB.

Test the complete application before making changes to the staging branch.

One important decision

If your cloned environment is going onto the same Ubuntu server, we need to make sure staging does not collide with production on:

Docker container names

ports

volumes

database

Nginx server blocks

environment files

uploaded files

cron/background workers

For example:

Production:
frontend → 3000
backend  → 5000
postgres → production DB

Staging:
frontend → 3001
backend  → 5001
postgres → staging DB

Nginx can then expose both through normal HTTPS domains, so you don't need users to access :3001 or :5001.

I would not copy the production .env wholesale. Copy the structure, then explicitly replace the database, secrets, storage, URLs, and any production-only integrations.

Response:

8/17/2026, 3:50:52 PM

Yes - I see what you started doing. The direction is right, but I would stop before continuing, because there are a few inconsistencies that will prevent the duplicate from becoming a clean staging environment.

What you changed correctly

You are separating staging from production by changing:

Backend port 5000 → 5500

Backend Docker EXPOSE

Backend server fallback port

Docker healthcheck

E2E port

PostgreSQL database name

Docker service names

That's the right general idea.

But there are 3 problems

Nginx is inconsistent

You changed the Docker Compose service from:

backend:

to:

backP:

but default.conf still has:

upstream backend {
    server backend:5500;
}

That will fail because Docker DNS will now know the service as backP, not backend.

It should be:

upstream backend {
    server backP:5500;
}

However, I wouldn't rename the service at all.

You don't actually need to change:

backend:
frontend:

Service names are isolated by the Compose project/network. You can run staging with a different Compose project name, so production can still have a backend service and staging can also have a backend service.

That's much cleaner.

Changing the frontend container's internal port is unnecessary

You changed:

frontend:

to:

frontP:

and:

expose:

"80"

to:

expose:

"880"

But your frontend Dockerfile/nginx is almost certainly listening on port 80 internally.

expose: 880 does not magically make nginx listen on 880.

So I would leave the frontend at port 80.

You only need to separate ports that are exposed on the host. If staging and production use separate Compose projects, they can both have:

frontend → port 80 internally
backend  → port 5000 internally

and Nginx routes to the correct containers.

Most importantly: don't change the application backend port just to separate environments

This:

-const port = process.env.PORT || 5000;
+const port = process.env.PORT || 5500;

isn't necessary.

Better:

const port = process.env.PORT || 5000;

Then staging's .env can specify:

PORT=5500

while production retains:

PORT=5000

That keeps the source code identical between environments.

Same principle applies to render.yaml, .env.example, tests, etc.

Environment differences should primarily live in environment configuration, not source code.

The bigger issue: your database change

You changed:

POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-creapyP}

That's okay as a fallback, but the real staging separation should happen in the staging .env.

For example:

POSTGRES_DB=creapy_staging

and:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://.../creapy_staging

You absolutely do not want staging accidentally connecting to the production database.

Also this:

file="/backups/creapyPs-$$(date...

looks like an accidental naming change (creapyPs). I'd make the staging backup name explicitly:

creapy-staging-...

What I recommend you do now

Since you've already cloned production, don't keep modifying the source to make it different.

Instead, make the clone staging through configuration:

Production clone
      │
      ├── same application code
      │
      ├── staging .env
      │      PORT=5500
      │      DATABASE_URL=staging DB
      │      JWT_SECRET=staging secret
      │      storage=staging
      │
      ├── staging compose project
      │
      └── staging nginx/domain

Then you can have:

Production
app.townruins.com
api.townruins.com

Staging
staging.townruins.com
staging-api.townruins.com

One more thing I noticed

Your diff contains ^M on several newly edited lines:

+PORT=5500^M

That's a CRLF line-ending change, probably because the file was edited on Windows. It isn't inherently fatal, but you don't want your staging conversion producing noisy line-ending changes throughout the repository.

So don't commit this diff yet.

If you want, I can work from the uploaded real-app-frontend-main.zip and identify the exact minimum files/lines that should change for staging, rather than you continuing to manually change ports/service names one by one.

nano docker-compose.staging.yml

Use:

services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-towruins_staging}
      POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER:?Set POSTGRES_USER}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - staging_pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $${POSTGRES_USER} -d $${POSTGRES_DB}"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    restart: unless-stopped

minio:
    image: minio/minio:latest
    command: server /data --console-address ":9001"
    environment:
      MINIO_ROOT_USER: ${MINIO_ROOT_USER:?Set MINIO_ROOT_USER}
      MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD:?Set MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD}
    volumes:
      - staging_minio_data:/data
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:9100:9000"
      - "127.0.0.1:9101:9001"
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl --fail http://localhost:9000/minio/health/live || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

postgres-backup:
    image: postgres:16
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      PGHOST: postgres
      PGPORT: "5432"
      PGDATABASE: ${POSTGRES_DB:-towruins_staging}
      PGUSER: ${POSTGRES_USER:?Set POSTGRES_USER}
      PGPASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS: ${POSTGRES_BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS:-14}
    volumes:
      - staging_pgbackups:/backups
    command:
      - sh
      - -c
      - |
        while true; do
          file="/backups/towruins-staging-$$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).dump"
          pg_dump -Fc --file="$$file"
          find /backups -type f -name '*.dump' -mtime +"$${BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS}" -delete
          sleep 86400
        done
    restart: unless-stopped

backend:
    build: ./backend
    env_file:
      - ./backend/.env.staging
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    expose:
      - "5500"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL:?Set DATABASE_URL}"
      JWT_SECRET: "${JWT_SECRET:?Set JWT_SECRET}"
      JWT_EXPIRES_IN: "${JWT_EXPIRES_IN:-30d}"
      COOKIE_SECRET: "${COOKIE_SECRET:?Set COOKIE_SECRET}"
      S3_BUCKET: "${S3_BUCKET:-townruins-staging}"
      S3_REGION: "${S3_REGION:-us-east-1}"
      S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID: "${S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID:?Set S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"
      S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: "${S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY:?Set S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}"
      S3_ENDPOINT: "${S3_ENDPOINT:-http://minio:9000}"
      S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL: "${S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL:-https://staging.townruins.com/creapy-uploads}"
      S3_BROWSER_ENDPOINT: "${S3_BROWSER_ENDPOINT:-https://staging.townruins.com}"
      S3_BROWSER_FORCE_PATH_STYLE: "${S3_BROWSER_FORCE_PATH_STYLE:-true}"
      PORT: "5500"
    volumes:
      - staging_uploads:/srv/uploads
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test:
        [
          "CMD",
          "node",
          "-e",
          "require('http').get('http://localhost:5500/', (res) => res.statusCode === 200 ? process.exit(0) : process.exit(1))"
        ]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    expose:
      - "80"
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- --timeout=2 --tries=1 http://127.0.0.1/ || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s

nginx:
    image: nginx:stable-alpine
    entrypoint: ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
    depends_on:
      backend:
        condition: service_healthy
      frontend:
        condition: service_healthy
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:80"
    volumes:
      - /etc/letsencrypt:/etc/letsencrypt:ro
      - ./docker/nginx/staging.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
      - staging_uploads:/srv/uploads:ro
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl --fail http://localhost/health || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3

volumes:
  staging_pgdata:
  staging_pgbackups:
  staging_uploads:
  staging_minio_data:

This gives staging its own:

Postgres volume
MinIO volume
uploads volume
backup volume
backend
frontend
nginx

while leaving production's Docker resources alone.

Create staging Nginx config

Create:

nano docker/nginx/staging.conf

Use:

upstream staging_backend {
    server backend:5500;
}

upstream staging_frontend {
    server frontend:80;
}

upstream staging_minio {
    server minio:9000;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name staging.townruins.com;

location /health {
    access_log off;
    return 200 'OK';
}

location /api/ {
    proxy_pass http://staging_backend;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Port $server_port;

    proxy_set_header Connection "";
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_redirect off;
}

location ^~ /creapy-uploads/ {
    proxy_pass http://staging_minio;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_request_buffering off;
    proxy_redirect off;
}

location / {
    proxy_pass http://staging_frontend;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

    proxy_buffering off;
}

}

Notice that this staging Nginx only binds:

127.0.0.1:8080

It does not touch production 80/443.

Configure the existing production Nginx as the edge

This is the part that matters most.

Your current production Nginx owns:

80
443

and currently serves:

api.townruins.com
townruins.com
app.townruins.com
www.townruins.com

as confirmed in the repository configuration.

We add a staging server block to the host/edge Nginx, forwarding:

staging.townruins.com
        ↓
127.0.0.1:8080
        ↓
staging nginx
        ↓
staging backend/frontend

But don't add this blindly yet.

First check where your current production Nginx configuration actually lives:

sudo nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -n -E 
'server_name|api.townruins.com|app.townruins.com|default.conf'

and:

docker compose ps

and:

docker ps --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Ports}}'

This will tell us whether the production Nginx is the Compose container shown in the repo or whether there is another host-level Nginx.

Create the staging DNS records

You will need:

staging.townruins.com

pointing to the same server IP as production.

If you also want a separate API hostname:

staging-api.townruins.com

I recommend doing that because it makes staging completely obvious.

Then your frontend/backend separation becomes:

PRODUCTION

https://app.townruins.com
https://api.townruins.com

STAGING

https://staging.townruins.com
https://staging-api.townruins.com

The architecture I recommend for your server

INTERNET
                            │
                            ▼
                    ┌───────────────┐
                    │ Production    │
                    │ Nginx :80/443 │
                    └───────┬───────┘
                            │
             ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
             │                             │
             ▼                             ▼
     production domains             staging.townruins.com
             │                             │
             ▼                             ▼
     Production Compose             127.0.0.1:8080
             │                             │
     ┌───────┴───────┐             Staging Nginx
     │               │                    │
 Backend 5000    Frontend 80       ┌──────┴──────┐
                                   │             │
                              Backend 5500   Frontend 80
                                   │
                              Staging DB

## Response:
8/17/2026, 3:50:52 PM

Yes - I see what you started doing. The direction is right, but I would stop before continuing, because there are a few inconsistencies that will prevent the duplicate from becoming a clean staging environment.

What you changed correctly

You are separating staging from production by changing:

Backend port 5000 → 5500

Backend Docker EXPOSE

Backend server fallback port

Docker healthcheck

E2E port

PostgreSQL database name

Docker service names

That's the right general idea.

But there are 3 problems

1. Nginx is inconsistent

You changed the Docker Compose service from:

backend:

to:

backP:

but default.conf still has:

upstream backend {
    server backend:5500;
}

That will fail because Docker DNS will now know the service as backP, not backend.

It should be:

upstream backend {
    server backP:5500;
}

However, I wouldn't rename the service at all.

You don't actually need to change:

backend:
frontend:

Service names are isolated by the Compose project/network. You can run staging with a different Compose project name, so production can still have a backend service and staging can also have a backend service.

That's much cleaner.

2. Changing the frontend container's internal port is unnecessary

You changed:

frontend:

to:

frontP:

and:

expose:
  - "80"

to:

expose:
  - "880"

But your frontend Dockerfile/nginx is almost certainly listening on port 80 internally.

expose: 880 does not magically make nginx listen on 880.

So I would leave the frontend at port 80.

You only need to separate ports that are exposed on the host. If staging and production use separate Compose projects, they can both have:

frontend → port 80 internally
backend  → port 5000 internally

and Nginx routes to the correct containers.

3. Most importantly: don't change the application backend port just to separate environments

This:

-const port = process.env.PORT || 5000;
+const port = process.env.PORT || 5500;

isn't necessary.

Better:

const port = process.env.PORT || 5000;

Then staging's .env can specify:

PORT=5500

while production retains:

PORT=5000

That keeps the source code identical between environments.

Same principle applies to render.yaml, .env.example, tests, etc.

Environment differences should primarily live in environment configuration, not source code.

The bigger issue: your database change

You changed:

POSTGRES_DB: ${POSTGRES_DB:-creapyP}

That's okay as a fallback, but the real staging separation should happen in the staging .env.

For example:

POSTGRES_DB=creapy_staging

and:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://.../creapy_staging

You absolutely do not want staging accidentally connecting to the production database.

Also this:

file="/backups/creapyPs-$$(date...

looks like an accidental naming change (creapyPs). I'd make the staging backup name explicitly:

creapy-staging-...

What I recommend you do now

Since you've already cloned production, don't keep modifying the source to make it different.

Instead, make the clone staging through configuration:

Production clone
      │
      ├── same application code
      │
      ├── staging .env
      │      PORT=5500
      │      DATABASE_URL=staging DB
      │      JWT_SECRET=staging secret
      │      storage=staging
      │
      ├── staging compose project
      │
      └── staging nginx/domain

Then you can have:

Production
app.townruins.com
api.townruins.com

Staging
staging.townruins.com
staging-api.townruins.com

One more thing I noticed

Your diff contains ^M on several newly edited lines:

+PORT=5500^M

That's a CRLF line-ending change, probably because the file was edited on Windows. It isn't inherently fatal, but you don't want your staging conversion producing noisy line-ending changes throughout the repository.

So don't commit this diff yet.

If you want, I can work from the uploaded real-app-frontend-main.zip and identify the exact minimum files/lines that should change for staging, rather than you continuing to manually change ports/service names one by one.

      retries: 5

      MINIO_ROOT_USER: ${MINIO_ROOT_USER:?Set MINIO_ROOT_USER}
      MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD:?Set MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD}

      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy

      PGPORT: "5432"

      PGPASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?Set POSTGRES_PASSWORD}

    volumes:
      - staging_pgbackups:/backups
    command:
      - sh
      - -c

        while true; do

          pg_dump -Fc --file="$$file"
          find /backups -type f -name '*.dump' -mtime +"$${BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS}" -delete
          sleep 86400
        done
    restart: unless-stopped

  backend:
    build: ./backend
    env_file:
      - ./backend/.env.staging
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    expose:
      - "5500"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: "${DATABASE_URL:?Set DATABASE_URL}"
      JWT_SECRET: "${JWT_SECRET:?Set JWT_SECRET}"
      JWT_EXPIRES_IN: "${JWT_EXPIRES_IN:-30d}"
      COOKIE_SECRET: "${COOKIE_SECRET:?Set COOKIE_SECRET}"
      S3_BUCKET: "${S3_BUCKET:-townruins-staging}"
      S3_REGION: "${S3_REGION:-us-east-1}"
      S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID: "${S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID:?Set S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"
      S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: "${S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY:?Set S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}"
      S3_ENDPOINT: "${S3_ENDPOINT:-http://minio:9000}"
      S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL: "${S3_PUBLIC_BASE_URL:-https://staging.townruins.com/creapy-uploads}"
      S3_BROWSER_ENDPOINT: "${S3_BROWSER_ENDPOINT:-https://staging.townruins.com}"
      S3_BROWSER_FORCE_PATH_STYLE: "${S3_BROWSER_FORCE_PATH_STYLE:-true}"
      PORT: "5500"
    volumes:
      - staging_uploads:/srv/uploads
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test:
        [
          "CMD",
          "node",
          "-e",
          "require('http').get('http://localhost:5500/', (res) => res.statusCode === 200 ? process.exit(0) : process.exit(1))"
        ]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    expose:
      - "80"
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "wget -qO- --timeout=2 --tries=1 http://127.0.0.1/ || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 10s

  nginx:
    image: nginx:stable-alpine
    entrypoint: ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
    depends_on:
      backend:
        condition: service_healthy
      frontend:
        condition: service_healthy
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:80"
    volumes:
      - /etc/letsencrypt:/etc/letsencrypt:ro
      - ./docker/nginx/staging.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
      - staging_uploads:/srv/uploads:ro
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl --fail http://localhost/health || exit 1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3

volumes:
  staging_pgdata:
  staging_pgbackups:
  staging_uploads:
  staging_minio_data:

This gives staging its own:

Postgres volume
MinIO volume
uploads volume
backup volume
backend
frontend
nginx

while leaving production's Docker resources alone.

5. Create staging Nginx config

Create:

nano docker/nginx/staging.conf

Use:

upstream staging_backend {
    server backend:5500;
}

upstream staging_frontend {
    server frontend:80;
}

upstream staging_minio {
    server minio:9000;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name staging.townruins.com;

    location /health {
        access_log off;
        return 200 'OK';
    }

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass http://staging_backend;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;

        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Port $server_port;

        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_buffering off;
        proxy_redirect off;
    }

    location ^~ /creapy-uploads/ {
        proxy_pass http://staging_minio;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;

        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

        proxy_buffering off;
        proxy_request_buffering off;
        proxy_redirect off;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://staging_frontend;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;

        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

        proxy_buffering off;
    }
}

Notice that this staging Nginx only binds:

127.0.0.1:8080

It does not touch production 80/443.

6. Configure the existing production Nginx as the edge

This is the part that matters most.

Your current production Nginx owns:

80
443

and currently serves:

api.townruins.com
townruins.com
app.townruins.com
www.townruins.com

as confirmed in the repository configuration.

We add a staging server block to the host/edge Nginx, forwarding:

staging.townruins.com
        ↓
127.0.0.1:8080
        ↓
staging nginx
        ↓
staging backend/frontend

But don't add this blindly yet.

First check where your current production Nginx configuration actually lives:

sudo nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -n -E \
'server_name|api.townruins.com|app.townruins.com|default.conf'

and:

docker compose ps

and:

docker ps --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Ports}}'

This will tell us whether the production Nginx is the Compose container shown in the repo or whether there is another host-level Nginx.

7. Create the staging DNS records

You will need:

staging.townruins.com

pointing to the same server IP as production.

If you also want a separate API hostname:

staging-api.townruins.com

I recommend doing that because it makes staging completely obvious.

Then your frontend/backend separation becomes:

PRODUCTION

https://app.townruins.com
https://api.townruins.com

STAGING

https://staging.townruins.com
https://staging-api.townruins.com

The architecture I recommend for your server

INTERNET
                            │

                    ┌───────────────┐

     │               │                    │

                                   │             │
                              Backend 5500   Frontend 80

                              Staging DB

## Response:
8/16/2026, 4:10:47 AM

If you mean vectorizing the database for Town Ruins—i.e. adding a vector/embedding layer so listings, descriptions, amenities, etc. can support semantic search—I can help you set that up.

Given your current PostgreSQL setup, the straightforward option is PostgreSQL + pgvector rather than introducing a separate vector database.

Typical architecture:

PostgreSQL
→ normal relational data
→ pgvector embedding columns
→ embeddings generated from listing/user/content text
→ cosine/inner-product similarity search
→ API endpoint for semantic search

For example, a listing could have an embedding representing:

“2-bedroom furnished apartment in Harare, secure parking, Wi-Fi, swimming pool…”

Then a user can search:

“comfortable furnished place with good internet and parking”

and retrieve semantically similar listings even without exact keyword matches.

If that's what you mean, send me the current DB/schema or let me inspect the uploaded project ZIP, and I can identify exactly where to add pgvector, the Prisma schema changes, embedding generation, indexing, and search API.

Scope
Backend: uploadController authorization and ownership validation for listing media

Summary

Root cause: uploadController restricted listing uploads to the landlord role only; the current domain model allows provider users to create/manage listings. Additionally, the controller used req.user._id which does not match the Prisma user.id in auth middleware, leading to inconsistent object keys.

Fix: Allowed roles for listings uploads are now landlord, provider and administrative roles (admin, super_admin). If a listingId is supplied the controller verifies the listing exists and belongs to the requesting user (unless admin). Also normalized user id extraction to use req.user.id || req.user._id and preserved existing content-type and folder allowlisting.

Tests: Updated unit test expectation and ran backend unit tests for the upload and monetization rules; relevant tests pass locally.

Diagnosing Signup Email Logs

Diagnosed signup email logs and inspected environment configuration safely

Yes — the logs show the signup request itself is working:

POST /api/v1/users/signup HTTP/2.0" 201

So this is not an nginx/frontend routing problem.

I also checked the backend source you uploaded, and there is a very strong culprit:

The verification flow is explicitly bypassed when this is true

SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true

Your backend's signup controller does this:

if (process.env.SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION === "true") {
    // marks the user as email verified
    // does NOT call sendVerificationEmail()
}

And your backend .env.example currently contains exactly:

SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true

The normal email path only happens when that value is not "true".

First, run this on the server

Don't paste the whole .env because it may contain passwords/secrets:

docker compose exec backend sh -lc '
echo "SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=$SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION"
echo "GMAIL_USER=$GMAIL_USER"
echo "EMAIL_FROM=$EMAIL_FROM"
echo "APP_BASE_URL=$APP_BASE_URL"
'

Also check the actual container environment:

docker compose exec backend env | grep -E '^(SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION|GMAIL_USER|EMAIL_FROM|APP_BASE_URL)='

What I expect

If you get:

SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true

then we have found the immediate reason.

Change it in the environment used by Docker to:

SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=false

Then recreate the backend:

docker compose up -d --force-recreate backend

Then verify:

docker compose exec backend sh -lc 'echo "SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=$SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION"'

It should say:

SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=false

But there's a second thing we should verify

Your email implementation is using Gmail SMTP:

service: "gmail",
auth: {
  user: process.env.GMAIL_USER,
  pass: process.env.GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD,
}

So after disabling the skip flag, test a new signup and immediately run:

docker compose logs backend --tail 100

If Gmail rejects the message, the backend should now return a 503 rather than pretending verification was sent.

One important security issue: the uploaded .env.example contains what appears to be a real Gmail app password. If that value is/was actually valid, revoke it and generate a new Gmail App Password. Don't commit the replacement credential to the repository.

The interesting part of your current nginx log is that signup returns 201, while there is no corresponding email error in the backend logs. Combined with the controller code, that makes SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true the first thing I'd check.

Run the docker compose exec backend ... command above and give me its output. We can then determine whether the SMTP layer is actually the next problem.

## Response:

Yes. What you’re describing is essentially an automated email operations system rather than just SMTP:

Inbox monitoring — detect new incoming mail automatically.

Classification — job application, recruiter, customer/user issue, provider issue, system alert, spam, etc.

AI-assisted replies — draft appropriate responses based on the email and previous thread.

Job applications — track applications, companies, roles, status, follow-ups and deadlines.

Issue handling — convert actionable emails into tracked issues/tickets, assign priority and status.

Automatic follow-ups — remind you when someone hasn't replied or an application needs attention.

Outbound automation — send approved responses and templated messages.

Audit trail — keep the original email, classification, actions taken and response history.

Town Ruins monitoring — your application can also send operational errors/alerts into the same system so an incoming issue can automatically become a tracked incident.

The architecture I'd recommend

Your Email
    │
    ▼
Email Integration
    │
    ├── Incoming mail
    │       │
    │       ▼
    │   AI Classifier
    │       │
    │       ├── Job application
    │       ├── Customer/user issue
    │       ├── Provider issue
    │       ├── System/technical alert
    │       └── Other
    │
    ▼
Automation / Rules Engine
    │
    ├── Create issue
    ├── Update existing issue
    ├── Draft reply
    ├── Schedule follow-up
    ├── Update application tracker
    └── Notify you
    │
    ▼
Dashboard / Issue Tracker

For your situation, I would not make the AI automatically send arbitrary emails from day one. I'd use:

Read → classify → track → draft → you approve → send

Then, once you've established that the classification and response quality are reliable, we can selectively automate low-risk responses.

For your Town Ruins project specifically

I'd actually integrate this with the existing backend rather than build a completely separate system.

You could have something like:

EmailEvent
 ├── messageId
 ├── threadId
 ├── sender
 ├── recipient
 ├── subject
 ├── receivedAt
 ├── category
 ├── priority
 ├── status
 ├── aiSummary
 ├── aiDraft
 └── relatedEntityId

Issue
 ├── id
 ├── source = EMAIL | SYSTEM | USER
 ├── category
 ├── priority
 ├── status
 ├── assignedTo
 ├── emailThreadId
 ├── createdAt
 └── resolvedAt

JobApplication
 ├── company
 ├── position
 ├── contact
 ├── applicationDate
 ├── status
 ├── nextFollowUp
 └── emailThreadId

That would give you a single operational inbox where an email from a Town Ruins user, an AWS alert, or a recruiter can all become trackable events.

The next step is choosing the actual email provider/integration (Gmail/Google Workspace, Outlook/Microsoft 365, etc.). Since this requires access to an external email account, I can check which integrations are available and recommend the smallest setup needed.

Yes - Zoho is actually a very good fit for what you're describing, especially because you want email + automation + issue tracking rather than just an SMTP server.

I’d structure your setup around Zoho Mail + Zoho Flow + Zoho Desk/CRM, rather than building the whole automation engine yourself.

Recommended setup

1. Zoho Mail - your email hub

Your mailbox receives everything:

job applications/recruiters

Town Ruins user issues

provider/landlord messages

AWS/server alerts

business correspondence

general enquiries

Zoho Flow can connect directly to Zoho Mail and has triggers for received mail, mail from particular senders, sent mail, and tagged mail. It can also create drafts, reply to messages, send mail, apply tags, create tasks and move messages between folders. (Zoho Corporation)

2. Zoho Flow - the automation brain

For example:

NEW EMAIL
   ↓
Classify
   ↓
┌──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
│ Job          │ Town Ruins   │ Other        │
│ application  │ issue        │              │
└──────┬───────┴──────┬───────┴──────────────┘
       ↓              ↓
Create application   Create issue
       ↓              ↓
Set follow-up        Set priority
       ↓              ↓
Draft reply          Draft response
       └───────┬──────┘
               ↓
          YOU APPROVE
               ↓
             SEND

Zoho Flow supports decisions, delays, custom functions and scheduled workflows, so you can build considerably more sophisticated logic than simple email filters. It also records flow execution history, which is useful when an automation fails. (Zoho Corporation)

3. Zoho Desk - automatic issue tracking

This is the piece I'd use for your "track issues as they arise" requirement.

For example:

User emails support@townruins.com

Flow can:

Email received
     ↓
Identify sender
     ↓
Check whether an existing issue/ticket exists
     ↓
Existing? ── YES → append to ticket
     │
     NO
     ↓
Create ticket
     ↓
Categorize
     ↓
Set priority
     ↓
Notify you

That means you don't have to manually remember that somebody emailed you three days ago about a problem.

Zoho's own CRM automation also supports creating cases from received emails, and Flow can connect these workflows to other applications. (Zoho Corporation)

4. Job applications become a separate pipeline

I'd keep job applications separate from support issues.

Something like:

Company
Position
Application date
Contact
Email thread
CV used
Cover letter
Status
Next follow-up
Interview date
Salary
Notes

Statuses:

FOUND
↓
APPLIED
↓
ACKNOWLEDGED
↓
INTERVIEW
↓
SECOND INTERVIEW
↓
OFFER
↓
ACCEPTED / REJECTED

Then automation can say:

"Application to XYZ has had no response for 7 days."

→ create a follow-up task
→ generate a follow-up email
→ notify you.

Zoho Flow supports scheduled triggers and delays, which makes these follow-up workflows possible. (Zoho Corporation)

The important part: don't fully automate sending initially

I'd configure the system in three levels.

Level 1 - automatic tracking

AI can automatically:

read/classify incoming mail

create issues

categorize them

assign priority

update job applications

schedule reminders

summarize conversations

Level 2 - automatic drafting

AI generates:

Suggested response

but doesn't send it.

You review → click/send.

Level 3 - selective automatic sending

After we know the system is reliable, allow automatic replies for very safe cases:

"We received your application."

"Your support request has been received."

verification/instruction emails

standard acknowledgements

status notifications

But keep things like job applications, negotiations, complaints and sensitive customer issues under your approval.

And we can connect this directly to Town Ruins

This is where I think it becomes particularly useful for you.

Your Town Ruins backend could send operational events into Zoho:

Town Ruins
    │
    ├── API error
    ├── failed payment
    ├── failed email
    ├── provider problem
    ├── user complaint
    ├── booking problem
    └── authentication problem
             │
             ▼
        Zoho Flow
             │
             ▼
        Zoho Desk
             │
             ▼
       Issue / Ticket
             │
             ├── Priority
             ├── Status
             ├── Assignment
             ├── History
             └── Notifications

Then email and application monitoring become part of the same operational system as your production platform.

And because Zoho Flow has execution history, you also get visibility into whether the automation itself failed. (Zoho Corporation)

What I'd build for you

I'd start with one Zoho automation stack:

Zoho Mail
→ incoming/outgoing email

Zoho Flow
→ automation/routing

Zoho Desk
→ Town Ruins support + technical issues

Zoho CRM
→ contacts + job/application/business tracking

AI layer
→ classification, summarization, reply drafting and prioritization

Then we can connect your existing Town Ruins backend through webhooks/API instead of duplicating your application's data.

Zoho Flow explicitly supports webhook triggers, custom functions and integrations, so it can sit between Town Ruins and the Zoho ecosystem. (Zoho Corporation)

If your Zoho account is already set up, I can walk you through configuring this from the Zoho side first, then we can wire your Town Ruins backend into it.

Sources:

Zoho Mail integration | Zoho Flow

## Prompt:
8/12/2026, 3:31:58 PM

is it possible that the seeded admin has no userid allowing login but nosession specific activity is allowed includig dashboard

## Response:
8/12/2026, 3:31:49 PM

Yes - that is absolutely possible, and given the behavior you've been seeing, it is actually one of the things I'd check.

There are two separate concepts that can get mixed together:

User identity - the database User record and its id/userId.

Authentication/session - the JWT/session created at login and what the frontend/backend uses afterward.

A seeded admin could theoretically have a valid email/password and be allowed through a login endpoint, while not having a valid/usable user ID in the resulting auth payload. Then you could get strange behavior like:

Login appears successful.

Admin dashboard loads because some admin routes only check role === "super_admin" or a generic authenticated flag.

Routes that require req.user.id, userId, or ownership/activity context fail.

User-specific activity, notifications, profile data, audit information, etc. don't work.

The browser may contain something like:
{
  "role": "super_admin",
  "phoneNumber": null,
  "isEmailVerified": true,
  "isPhoneVerified": true,
  "verificationStatus": "UNVERIFIED"
}

but no id / userId.

However, there's an important distinction:

If the database User itself has no ID

That would be a database/schema problem. With Prisma, if User.id is required and generated by the database/application, a normal User row shouldn't exist without one.

If the database User has an ID but the JWT/session doesn't contain it

This is much more likely.

For example, the login code might create a token from:

{
  email: user.email,
  role: user.role
}

instead of:

{
  userId: user.id,
  email: user.email,
  role: user.role
}

Then the authentication middleware reconstructs:

req.user = {
  email,
  role
}

and anything doing:

req.user.id

gets undefined.

That would explain why dashboard access can work while user-specific operations don't.

The fastest way to prove it

Don't change anything yet. Check the seeded admin in PostgreSQL:

SELECT id, email, role, "isEmailVerified", "verificationStatus"
FROM "User"
WHERE email = 'YOUR_ADMIN_EMAIL';

Then compare that id with the actual JWT/session payload in the browser.

If the DB says:

id = abc123
email = admin@...
role = super_admin

but the browser token/session contains:

{
  "email": "admin@...",
  "role": "super_admin"
}

with no userId/id, we've found a very strong candidate for the problem.

And since you said earlier that you don't have Redux, I would specifically inspect the actual login response/token and the auth middleware rather than looking for Redux state.

If you want, we can trace this from seeded admin → login endpoint → JWT creation → auth middleware → dashboard request and identify exactly where the user ID disappears.

## Prompt:
8/12/2026, 3:34:21 PM

what if user id id is associated with the username seed only sets email and password

## Response:
8/12/2026, 3:34:12 PM

Yes — that could be the issue, depending on how your schema and authentication code work.

If your User model has something like:

model User {
  id       String @id @default(uuid())
  username String @unique
  email    String @unique
  password String
  ...
}

then seeding only:

{
  email: "admin@townruins.com",
  password: hashedPassword
}

would not normally mean the id is missing. Prisma would generate the id automatically if @default(uuid()) is defined.

But if your application has logic where username is required for authentication/session creation, then the seed can create a user that exists in the database but isn't fully compatible with the normal login flow.

For example, login might do:

const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({
  where: { email }
});

and then later:

const token = jwt.sign({
  userId: user.id,
  username: user.username,
  role: user.role
}, JWT_SECRET);

If username is null/missing, the token generation or subsequent user/session logic could behave differently.

This is especially worth checking in your case

You previously encountered:

PrismaClientValidationError
missing username in prisma.user.create

So I would not assume username is optional in your application's actual flow, even if the database technically allows the row.

The important thing is to inspect the seed and schema together:

grep -n "model User" -A80 prisma/schema.prisma

and:

grep -R "prisma.user.create\|prisma.user.upsert" -n . --exclude-dir=node_modules

Then check the actual seeded record:

SELECT
  id,
  username,
  email,
  role,
  "isEmailVerified",
  "verificationStatus"
FROM "User"
WHERE email = 'YOUR_ADMIN_EMAIL';

If you get something like:

id        = abc-123
username  = NULL
email     = admin@townruins.com
role      = super_admin

then the user ID exists, but the user is incomplete relative to what your application expects.

That could absolutely produce the situation you're describing: the admin can authenticate enough to reach the dashboard, but operations that depend on a properly identified user fail.

So I would check id + username + role + the login JWT payload before changing the authentication code.

## Prompt:
8/14/2026, 10:35:58 AM

y {
      const user: any = await updateProfile({
        id: userId,
        payload,
      });

That snippet right there is the smoking gun causing the issue! Look at what you're passing to updateProfile vs what userApiSlice.ts expects:

The Mismatch

In your component, you are passing:

TypeScript

updateProfile({
  id: userId,
  payload,
})

This creates an object shaped like this:

JSON

{
  "id": "cmsp6gvgt00005nfntjc5dck8",
  "payload": { ...formFields }
}

However, inside userApiSlice.ts, your endpoint query is written as:

TypeScript

update: builder.mutation({
  query: (data) => {
    return {
      url: `users/update/${data.id}`,
      method: "PUT",
      body: data, // <--- Sends the entire payload object as body
    };
  },
}),

Because updateProfile was being passed an object where the user properties were nested inside payload (or because data expected flat object fields), sending { id, payload } results in sending { id, payload } as the request body rather than flat user data, and if id isn't structured properly on data, data.id resolves improperly or fails to map!

The Fix

You have two clean options depending on how your backend expects the request body:

Option 1: Flatten the payload in the caller (Recommended if backend expects flat fields)

Pass userId flattened directly into the payload object when calling updateProfile:

TypeScript

try {
  const user = await updateProfile({
    id: userId,
    ...payload, // Flattens payload properties at top level alongside id
  }).unwrap();
  
  console.log("Profile updated successfully:", user);
} catch (error) {
  console.error("Update failed:", error);
}

Option 2: Adjust userApiSlice.ts (If you want to keep { id, payload })

If you want your component to keep passing { id: userId, payload }, update userApiSlice.ts to unwrap payload for the HTTP request body:

TypeScript

// src/redux/api/userApiSlice.ts

update: builder.mutation({
  query: ({ id, payload }) => {
    return {
      url: `users/update/${id}`,
      method: "PUT",
      body: payload, // Sends only the form fields in the request body
    };
  },
}),

Quick Recap

Why it failed: userApiSlice.ts accessed data.id expecting data to be a flat object, but the component was passing { id, payload }.

Bonus tip: Always append .unwrap() when calling RTK Query mutations with await so you catch actual response errors in your try...catch block!

## Response:
8/13/2026, 5:11:43 AM

Yes — this is the right approach for giving the new developer server access without handing over your PEM file.

For your situation, I would simplify it considerably. You don't need to send them all those references or explanations. Just give them the few commands they need.

If they're on Windows using PowerShell, the process is essentially:

They run:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "their-email@example.com"

They press Enter to accept the default location and set a passphrase.

Then they send you only:

id_ed25519.pub

You add their public key on the Ubuntu server:

mkdir -p ~/.ssh
nano ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Paste their .pub key on a new line, save, then:

chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Then they connect with:

ssh ubuntu@YOUR_SERVER_IP

The important distinction is:

✅ They send you id_ed25519.pub

❌ They never send you id_ed25519

❌ They don't need your .pem

❌ You don't need their private key

One thing I'd change for your AWS setup

Since you're using an Ubuntu EC2 instance, if you're currently logging in as ubuntu with your AWS .pem, don't create their key under your own account's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys unless that's actually the account you want them sharing.

A cleaner setup is to give the developer their own Linux user, e.g.:

sudo adduser developer
sudo mkdir -p /home/developer/.ssh
sudo nano /home/developer/.ssh/authorized_keys

Paste their public key, then:

sudo chown -R developer:developer /home/developer/.ssh
sudo chmod 700 /home/developer/.ssh
sudo chmod 600 /home/developer/.ssh/authorized_keys

They then connect with:

ssh developer@YOUR_SERVER_IP

That's preferable for a two-person team because you can later remove their access without affecting yours, and you can see which Linux account performed actions.

If you're going to give them fairly broad access to the Town Ruins server, I'd also avoid making them root immediately. We can set up the developer account with the exact Docker/Git/deployment permissions they need.

8/11/2026, 9:42:11 AM

These logs actually look mostly healthy. I don't see a backend crash or an Nginx → backend connectivity problem.

What the logs tell us

1. Backend is running correctly

The important sequence is:

Connected to Aurora PostgreSQL
Environment: production
Server running on port 5000

Prisma also generated successfully:

✔ Generated Prisma Client (v5.22.0)

So:

Docker backend is up

Prisma is working

Aurora PostgreSQL is reachable

Node server is listening on 5000

Scheduled workers initialized

2. Your API requests are reaching Nginx successfully

For example:

OPTIONS /api/v1/notifications/unread-count HTTP/2.0 204
GET /api/v1/notifications/unread-count HTTP/2.0 304

And later:

POST /api/v1/users/login HTTP/2.0 200

That's particularly important: login is returning HTTP 200.

The dashboard endpoints are also responding:

GET /api/v1/users/wallet/balance 304
GET /api/v1/users/wallet/transactions?limit=50 304
GET /api/v1/listings/stats 304
GET /api/v1/listings/home/highlighted?limit=6 304

So the request chain appears to be:

Browser
   ↓
app.townruins.com
   ↓
Nginx
   ↓
Backend :5000
   ↓
Aurora PostgreSQL

and that chain is functioning.

3. 304 is NOT an error

This is important because there are a lot of them.

304 Not Modified

means the browser/cache already has the resource and the server says:

"Nothing has changed; use what you already have."

So this:

GET /api/v1/users/wallet/balance 304

does not mean the API failed.

Likewise:

GET /api/v1/notifications/unread-count 304

is normal HTTP caching behavior.

4. CORS preflight is also working

You have:

OPTIONS ... 204

for the API calls.

That's exactly what we'd expect from browser CORS preflight.

So the earlier authorization/CORS issue doesn't appear to be manifesting as an Nginx-level failure here.

The thing I would investigate

There is a very suspicious pattern:

OPTIONS /api/v1/notifications/unread-count
GET     /api/v1/notifications/unread-count

repeating approximately every few seconds.

And your localhost health check is doing:

GET / HTTP/1.1 301

every ~10 seconds.

The ::1 requests are almost certainly your Docker/container health check or local monitoring.

The browser requests, however, appear to be repeatedly polling:

/api/v1/notifications/unread-count

So if your concern is why the system is generating constant requests / why the dashboard keeps refreshing / why the backend appears busy, I'd look at the frontend notification polling.

Also: these are internet scanners, not your application

These are unrelated external probes:

GET /wp-admin/install.php?step=1

and:

GET /developmentserver/metadatauploader

The second one returned:

404

That's good.

The wp-admin request got:

301

because your Nginx configuration redirected it, rather than exposing anything.

These are normal background internet scans against public IPs/domains. Don't build application functionality around these requests.

One warning you should eventually address

Your backend is running:

node v20.20.2

while AWS SDK is warning that future versions will require Node 22:

versions published after the first week of January 2027
will require node >=22

That's not causing today's problem. But I'd put upgrading the Docker image to Node 22 on the maintenance list.

listings       → 304
stats          → 304

There are zero 401/403/404/500 responses in this HAR.

The real clue is inside your deployed JavaScript

I searched the actual main.6594c567.js captured by the HAR.

Your application does have an /dashboard/admin route:

/dashboard/admin
allowedRoles: ["admin", "super_admin"]

So the route wasn't forgotten.

More importantly, the route is wrapped in your authorization component.

The deployed code effectively does this:

if user exists:
    if user's role is allowed:
        render admin dashboard
    else:
        redirect to role's dashboard
else:
    redirect to /login

And the role routing is:

admin / super_admin → /dashboard/admin
landlord             → /dashboard/landlord
provider             → /dashboard/provider
tenant               → /dashboard/tenant
anything else        → /

That's directly visible in the deployed bundle.

Therefore the most likely problem is:

The frontend's authenticated user state does not contain admin or super_admin as the role when /dashboard/admin is opened.

The guard then redirects away from /dashboard/admin.

And the HAR strongly supports that conclusion because after loading /dashboard/admin, the requests are coming from:

https://app.townruins.com/

rather than:

https://app.townruins.com/dashboard/admin

That's why you're seeing the normal homepage/general APIs.

There is another important issue

Your HAR doesn't contain a login request.

The first request is already:

GET /dashboard/admin

and the subsequent API requests don't show an Authorization header in the HAR.

That means we need to determine exactly what the browser believes the current authenticated user is.

Given the code we've already been looking at in this project, I would not change Nginx or Docker yet.

The problem is now looking strongly like:

JWT/login response
       ↓
auth state/localStorage
       ↓
user.role
       ↓
$S authorization guard
       ↓
/dashboard/admin rejected
       ↓
redirect
       ↓
homepage

One thing I would check immediately

On the browser where you're trying /dashboard/admin, open DevTools → Console and run:

JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user"))

If that returns an object, look specifically at:

JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user"))?.role

and:

JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user"))?.user?.role

One of those is likely going to expose the issue.

Also run:

Object.keys(localStorage)

We want to see whether the deployed frontend is storing the user in the structure that your current authSlice.ts expects.

Why I think this is more likely than the backend

Your backend is clearly alive:

Connected to Aurora PostgreSQL
Environment: production
Server running on port 5000

And the HAR proves the API is responding successfully.

Even more importantly, if the backend were rejecting the admin request, I'd expect to see something like:

GET /api/v1/admin/... → 401

or:

GET /api/v1/admin/... → 403

But there are no admin API requests at all.

The React authorization guard is apparently stopping you before the admin dashboard component ever gets to make its API calls.

One more thing: don't confuse this with the email issue

The HAR also doesn't tell us why email isn't being sent. The resend-verification request isn't present in this HAR, and your server logs only show:

POST /api/v1/users/resend-verification → 200

A 200 there means the endpoint accepted the request; it does not prove Gmail successfully delivered the message.

That's a separate backend/email investigation.

For the admin dashboard problem, though, the evidence is quite strong:

The deployed frontend recognizes /dashboard/admin, but the authorization guard is redirecting the current user away from it because the frontend auth state isn't resolving that user as admin or super_admin.

The next thing I'd inspect is the actual localStorage.user value and the login response.

No 401, 403, or 500 appears in the nginx logs you posted.

So I would not start by changing JWT/authentication.

What stands out

The important missing piece is what happens after navigating to /dashboard/admin. Your nginx excerpt doesn't contain a request for:

/dashboard/admin

That suggests the problem may be frontend-side routing/authorization, rather than the backend rejecting the admin user.

There is also an important distinction:

localStorage.user
└── data
    ├── data
    │   └── user
    │       └── role: "super_admin"
    ├── status: "success"
    └── token: "..."

If the frontend's admin route guard is expecting something like:

user.role

instead of:

user.data.user.role

it could incorrectly conclude that the logged-in user isn't an admin.

However, I don't want to guess at that without inspecting the HAR/code.

One security issue first

Rotate that JWT. You pasted an active authentication token into the conversation. Even though it is temporary/expiring, treat it as compromised and log the account out / invalidate the session after debugging.

Next thing I would inspect

The HAR should tell us exactly which of these is happening:

/dashboard/admin loads but React redirects away.

The admin page loads but an API call returns 401/403.

An admin API call isn't being made at all.

The frontend sends the JWT but the role is read from the wrong object.

The admin dashboard chunk/route fails to load.

A Redux/localStorage hydration issue causes the route guard to see an unauthenticated user briefly/permanently.

Your production checklist also explicitly expects the backend JWT configuration (JWT_SECRET, expiration, etc.) and a seeded super-admin account, while the email configuration is separate (GMAIL_USER, GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD, EMAIL_FROM). Pasted text.txt Pasted text.txt

So the evidence currently points much more strongly toward the frontend admin-route/session handling than the email problem or basic authentication.

Investigation summary (concise)

Root cause (most likely)

Frontend fetchBaseQuery prepareHeaders is broken: frontend/src/redux/api/apiSlice.ts sets the Authorization header incorrectly (the token is masked/removed). This prevents sending a valid Authorization header so admin API calls are unauthenticated (or not attempted as the app logic short-circuits).

Key evidence in code

apiSlice.prepareHeaders (frontend/src/redux/api/apiSlice.ts)
Lines ~10–16: reads token from state, then:
headers.set("authorization", `******;

This is a direct bug: the header assignment is not setting Bearer ${token}.

authSlice stores/reads localStorage "user" (frontend/src/redux/auth/authSlice.ts):
parseStoredUser() reads localStorage.getItem("user")

getStoredUserToken() returns storedUser?.token ?? storedUser?.data?.token

Login writes localStorage "user" (frontend/src/views/Login/index.tsx):
localStorage.setItem("user", JSON.stringify(user));

Admin component mounts and calls admin hooks unconditionally:
frontend/src/views/Dashboard/Admin.tsx calls useGetAdminUsersQuery({ page:1, limit:50 }) at top-level (so it should generate a network request).

Exact execution flow causing the failure

Browser navigates to /dashboard/admin — static frontend route loads (hence HTTP 200 for the HTML/JS/CSS).

React mounts Admin component. The component executes hooks (useGetAdminUsersQuery, useGetLegalDocsQuery, etc.).

RTK Query uses apiSlice.fetchBaseQuery → prepareHeaders runs to add Authorization from Redux state.

prepareHeaders, as coded, does not set a valid Authorization header (the code sets a masked/invalid value). Therefore either:
no Authorization header arrives at the backend OR

an invalid header arrives that the backend rejects.

Backend rejects authentication for protected admin endpoints; frontend either receives 401 or (depending on app logic) treats the response as unauthenticated and won’t render admin content. HAR shows no Authorization header and no admin-specific API traffic → implies either prepareHeaders returned no header OR the token in state was null.

Why the HAR shows the observed behavior

HTML/CSS/JS assets load from the server (public SPA) — that explains the 200 and successful chunk loads.

No admin-specific API requests observed:
Two reasons are possible (ranked):
prepareHeaders/RTK Query fails early or returns no effective header AND the client-side code observes missing token/role and avoids calling or hides admin behavior (but in this code hooks are invoked unconditionally — yet if getState().auth.user is null the token is undefined and header omitted).

The token is not present in Redux/localStorage (auth state lost or not hydrated), so prepareHeaders has nothing to send and network requests for admin endpoints are made without Authorization; depending on dev tools, those unauthenticated requests might be suppressed or collapsed in HAR view (or the UI requests are conditional and therefore not sent).

The broken literal in apiSlice is direct evidence that the header code was accidentally modified, so the missing Authorization makes most sense as the immediate cause.

Distinguishing evidence to gather (quick checks)

Inspect browser localStorage after authentication: is there a "user" key? Does it contain token at top-level or in data.token?

Open Console/Network and reload /dashboard/admin: do outgoing admin API requests appear? If they appear, do they include Authorization header? If they are absent, check whether React mounted Admin and whether hooks were invoked (console.log in component).

Inspect built/served JS (the actual deployed bundle) to confirm whether apiSlice in production matches source repo (maybe a build/use mismatch).

Recommended fix (small, surgical)

Restore proper header setting in apiSlice.prepareHeaders:
Retrieve token from state the same way auth selectors expect (e.g., authState?.token ?? authState?.data?.token).

Set header: headers.set("authorization", Bearer ${token});

Verify authSlice/localStorage usage is consistent:
Confirm login and other auth flows write the token into localStorage in the shape parseStoredUser expects (the code already writes localStorage.setItem("user", JSON.stringify(user)); and authSlice reads user?.token or user?.data?.token — ensure login response shape matches).

Add a brief defensive guard in prepareHeaders:
If token undefined, do not set header (current behavior), but ensure no masking or invalid literal is used.

Add a unit test or runtime console log to assert prepareHeaders returns expected header when store contains token (dev step).

Files to change

frontend/src/redux/api/apiSlice.ts — fix prepareHeaders to set Bearer ${token} correctly.

(Optional validation) frontend/src/redux/auth/authSlice.ts — confirm token selectors are correct / consistent with server response.

(Optional) small dev-only console.log in Admin.tsx or apiSlice to verify token at runtime.

Risks / regressions

Low-risk if change is exactly replacing the masked literal with proper Bearer token format. Possible regressions:
If production build intentionally masked tokens in source (unlikely), ensure no secrets are committed.

If some endpoints expect a different header name or format (rare); the project already used Authorization elsewhere so Bearer is expected.

If any other code assumes Authorization header is missing, those flows may change (but that would be normal, enabling authenticated access).

Concrete validation/test plan

Local quick dev check:
Start frontend dev server (npm start), log in as admin, open DevTools → Application → localStorage → inspect "user" object; ensure token exists (top-level or data.token).

In DevTools Network, navigate to /dashboard/admin; confirm GET /api/v1/admin/users is issued and its Request Headers include:
   Authorization: Bearer

Confirm endpoint returns 200 and UI displays admin data.

Automated checks:
Add a unit test for apiSlice.prepareHeaders behavior (mock store with auth.user containing token; call prepareHeaders and assert headers.get('authorization') === Bearer ${token}).

End-to-end:
Run frontend build + backend, log in as admin, exercise Admin Dashboard flows: list, search, open user, open legal docs.

Confirm API calls succeed and UI renders.

CI:
Run npm run build and frontend tests to ensure no TypeScript or lint errors.

Multiple plausible causes (ranked) and how to distinguish them

prepareHeaders corrupted (most likely)
Evidence: apiSlice shows headers.set("authorization", `******;).

Distinguish: fix this line and retry — if admin APIs start sending Authorization header and dashboards load, root cause confirmed.

Auth state not hydrated / localStorage key mismatch
Evidence: parseStoredUser expects localStorage "user". Login writes "user". Possible shape mismatch (token in nested data vs top-level).

Distinguish: check localStorage in browser; if no user key or no token, then hydration is the issue.

Admin component short-circuits (role check) before issuing API calls
Evidence: Admin.tsx does call hooks unconditionally; less likely.

Distinguish: add console.log in Admin mount or inspect whether hooks are invoked (network tabs).

CORS / proxy stripping Authorization header (unlikely)
Evidence: server config in backend/app.js sets Cors allowed headers including Authorization; Nginx might strip headers in some deployments.

Distinguish: check network requests directly to backend from browser; if Authorization was present in request to frontend host but missing to API origin, check server/proxy logs.

## Response:
8/10/2026, 5:19:06 PM

This is a TypeScript RTK Query tag-type mismatch, not a React build problem.

Your new getTemporaryStays endpoint returns:

{ type: "TemporaryStay", id: item._id }

but "TemporaryStay" is not registered in the API's tagTypes union.

Fix

Have Codex/Solai inspect the API slice where createApi(...) is defined and add TemporaryStay to the existing tagTypes array.

For example, if it currently has something like:

tagTypes: [

The important distinction is that 304 is not an error. It means the client's cached representation is still valid.

One thing I would investigate

You have a very regular sequence:

::1 → GET / → 301

every ~10 seconds:

06:59:38
06:59:48
06:59:58
07:00:08
...
07:01:29
07:01:39

At the same time the frontend has:

127.0.0.1 → GET / → 200

every ~10 seconds.

That strongly looks like Docker/container health checks rather than real users.

So this:

nginx → GET / → 301
frontend → GET / → 200

is probably your health-check chain. The 301 deserves checking because Nginx is redirecting /, but if the container health check follows the redirect or is configured to tolerate it, it's harmless.

The AWS SDK warning

This:

NodeVersionSupportWarning:
The AWS SDK for JavaScript (v3) versions published after
the first week of January 2027 will require node >=22.
You are running node v20.20.2.

is only a warning right now.

Your backend is successfully starting:

Connected to Aurora PostgreSQL
Environment: production
Server running on port 5000

So don't destabilize the production container just to address that warning. Node 22 should eventually be part of your planned runtime upgrade.

More importantly

The logs stop just after:

GET /api/v1/users/wallet/transactions?limit=50 → 304

If you're investigating one of the problems we've been working on—provider listing uploads, admin users/legal docs, Temporary Stay CRUD, or provider listing visibility—this particular excerpt doesn't show the failing request.

I'd run:

docker compose logs -f nginx backend --tail 100

then reproduce the exact failing action once in the browser.

For example, if testing the provider upload problem, watch specifically for:

POST /api/v1/uploads/r2-sign

and then immediately inspect backend output.

If you see:

POST /api/v1/uploads/r2-sign 403

that confirms the authorization issue we identified earlier.

If you see:

POST /api/v1/uploads/r2-sign 200

then we've moved past authorization and should follow the upload flow to R2/storage and listing persistence.

Don't restart anything based on this log alone. The stack shown here is up and serving requests normally.

## Response:
8/10/2026, 5:49:02 PM

Yes — these logs are actually quite useful. Nginx itself looks healthy. The requests are reaching your server, CORS preflights are succeeding, most API routes are working, and the errors are concentrated in a few backend endpoints.

The important distinction is:

Nginx is mostly doing its job. The 404/400/500 responses are coming from the application/backend behind Nginx, not from Nginx failing to route traffic.

1. What docker compose logs -f --tail 0 nginx means

docker compose logs -f --tail 0 nginx

logs → show container logs

-f → continuously follow new logs

--tail 0 → don't show old logs; only new requests

nginx → specifically the Nginx container

So you're watching live HTTP traffic hitting your production reverse proxy.

2. The overall picture

Your traffic flow is approximately:

Browser
   │
   │ HTTPS
   ▼
app.townruins.com
   │
   ▼
Nginx container
   │
   ├── /                 → frontend
   │
   └── /api/v1/*         → backend API container
                              │
                              ▼
                           Prisma/DB/etc.

The logs show that this entire chain is mostly functioning.

For example:

GET /api/v1/bookings HTTP/2.0" 200

means:

Browser
  ↓
Cloudflare / network
  ↓
Nginx
  ↓
Backend
  ↓
Database
  ↓
200 response

That's a successful end-to-end request.

3. OPTIONS ... 204 is GOOD

You're seeing a lot of:

OPTIONS /api/v1/providers HTTP/2.0" 204

and:

OPTIONS /api/v1/admin/users?page=1&limit=50 HTTP/2.0" 204

These are CORS preflight requests.

The browser is essentially asking:

"I'm https://app.townruins.com. Am I allowed to make this API request?"

Nginx/backend responds:

204 No Content

That means:

Yes, preflight accepted.

So this is not an error.

In fact, the fact that you are getting:

OPTIONS ... 204
GET ... 200

is strong evidence that your CORS configuration is working.

4. 304 is also normally GOOD

You're seeing things like:

GET /api/v1/notifications/unread-count HTTP/2.0" 304

and:

GET /api/v1/users/wallet/balance HTTP/2.0" 304

304 Not Modified means the browser already has a cached version and the server is telling it:

"Nothing changed. Use what you already have."

So:

304

does not mean your API failed.

It's normal HTTP caching behavior.

5. Your admin dashboard is loading successfully

This:

GET /dashboard/admin HTTP/2.0" 200

is important.

It means the frontend route itself loaded successfully.

Then the frontend starts calling APIs.

You have:

GET /api/v1/bookings HTTP/2.0" 200

GET /api/v1/users/wallet/balance HTTP/2.0" 304

GET /api/v1/users/wallet/transactions?limit=50 HTTP/2.0" 304

GET /api/v1/admin/temporary-stays?... HTTP/2.0" 200

So the admin dashboard is communicating with the backend.

That's a very good sign.

Problem A — 404 legal docs

Problem B — 404 admin users
