7. The 404s are NOT an Nginx problem

Take:

GET /api/v1/admin/legal-docs HTTP/2.0" 404 81

If Nginx couldn't find the route because of its own configuration, we'd investigate Nginx routing.

But look at your other API requests:

GET /api/v1/bookings → 200
GET /api/v1/providers → 304
GET /api/v1/users/wallet/balance → 304
GET /api/v1/admin/temporary-stays → 200

The /api/v1 proxy is clearly working.

Therefore the likely situation is:

Frontend
   ↓
GET /api/v1/admin/legal-docs
   ↓
Nginx
   ↓
Backend
   ↓
Backend doesn't have this route
   ↓
404

Likely causes:

Possibility 1

Frontend expects:

/api/v1/admin/legal-docs

but backend actually exposes something like:

/api/v1/legal-docs

Possibility 2

The backend route hasn't been implemented.

Possibility 3

The route exists in source code but isn't mounted.

For example, something like:

app.use('/api/v1/admin', adminRoutes);

but legal-docs wasn't added to adminRoutes.

Possibility 4

Frontend and backend are from different versions.

This is actually something I'd investigate strongly given your recent deployment/build work.

8. The admin users endpoint is the same story

You have:

GET /api/v1/admin/users?page=1&limit=50 HTTP/2.0" 404

The frontend expects:

GET /api/v1/admin/users

but the backend says:

404

Again:

Nginx is successfully forwarding the request.

The backend doesn't appear to recognize that route.

9. The invitations endpoint is more serious

This one:

GET /api/v1/admin/invitations HTTP/2.0" 500 57

is different.

500 means:

The backend encountered an internal server error while processing the request.

Unlike the 404:

404 → route/resource not found

a 500 means:

route exists
       ↓
backend started processing
       ↓
something crashed/failed
       ↓
500

This is the one where I'd immediately check the backend container logs.

Run:

docker compose logs --tail 200 backend

If your service isn't called backend, first run:

docker compose ps

and identify the API container.

Then:

docker compose logs --tail 200 <backend-service-name>

Or watch it live:

docker compose logs -f <backend-service-name>

Then reproduce:

GET /api/v1/admin/invitations

The backend log should reveal the actual exception.

13. ::1 GET / → 301 is probably your Docker health check

You repeatedly have:

::1 - - ... "GET / HTTP/1.1" 301 ... "curl/8.21.0"

That's almost certainly an internal Docker/container health check or monitoring request.

::1 means IPv6 localhost:

::1 = localhost

And:

curl/8.21.0

means something inside the environment is using curl.

The:

301

means Nginx redirects / somewhere else, probably HTTPS or another configured path.

Not concerning by itself.

14. Cloudflare is probably in front of you

This line:

172.68.42.86

is consistent with Cloudflare infrastructure, while Nginx is also showing:

197.221.251.65

and:

102.128.76.248

Your final quoted IP field sometimes contains:

"197.221.251.65"

That suggests your Nginx configuration may be handling proxy headers such as:

X-Forwarded-For
X-Real-IP
CF-Connecting-IP

So your architecture may effectively be:

User
 ↓
Cloudflare
 ↓
Nginx
 ↓
Docker API
 ↓
Prisma
 ↓
Database

That's normal.

16. The next thing I'd do

Don't change Nginx yet.

First inspect the backend errors.

Run:

docker compose ps

Then identify your API/backend service and run:

docker compose logs --tail 200 <backend-service>

Even better, reproduce the invitations error while watching:

docker compose logs -f <backend-service>

Then refresh the admin dashboard.

We're looking specifically for the exception generated immediately after:

GET /api/v1/admin/invitations

Also test the 404 routes directly from the server:

curl -i https://app.townruins.com/api/v1/admin/legal-docs
curl -i https://app.townruins.com/api/v1/admin/users?page=1\&limit=50
curl -i https://app.townruins.com/api/v1/admin/invitations

And for the DELETE 400:

curl -i -X DELETE \
  https://app.townruins.com/api/v1/admin/temporary-stays/cmsnb0m9m000lvvtv7nq7z6eb

Don't worry about the 204s and 304s. Those are mostly signs that things are working.

The three things worth chasing now are why the frontend is requesting two routes the backend doesn't recognize, why invitations is throwing 500, and why certain temporary stays are being rejected with 400.

const crypto = require("crypto");
const csv = require("csv-parse/sync");
const bcrypt = require("bcryptjs");
const { v4: uuidv4 } = require("uuid");

const catchAsync = require("../utils/catchAsync");
const prisma = require("../utils/prisma");
const AppError = require("../utils/appError");
const { sendEmail, buildBrandedEmail } = require("../utils/email");
const auditLog = require("../utils/auditLog");

const VALID_ROLES = ["tenant", "landlord", "provider"];
const CLAIM_TOKEN_EXPIRY_HOURS = 7 * 24; // 7 days
const SALT_ROUNDS = 10;

const getAppBaseUrl = () => {
const configuredBaseUrl =
process.env.APP_BASE_URL || process.env.FRONTEND_URL || "http://localhost:3000";
return configuredBaseUrl.replace(//+$/, "");
};

const generateClaimToken = () => {
const rawToken = crypto.randomBytes(32).toString("hex");
const hashedToken = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(rawToken).digest("hex");
return { rawToken, hashedToken };
};

const validateEmail = (email) => {
const emailRegex = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+.[^\s@]+$/;
return emailRegex.test(email);
};

const validateRole = (role) => {
return VALID_ROLES.includes(role?.toLowerCase());
};

const parseCSV = (fileBuffer) => {
try {
const content = fileBuffer.toString("utf-8");
const records = csv.parse(content, {
columns: true,
skip_empty_lines: true,
trim: true,
relax_column_count: true,
});
return records;
} catch (error) {
throw new AppError(CSV parsing failed: ${error.message}, 400);
}
};

const validateRow = async (row, rowNumber, existingEmails) => {
const errors = [];
const data = {};

// Email validation
if (!row.email || !row.email.trim()) {
errors.push("Email is required");
} else if (!validateEmail(row.email.trim())) {
errors.push("Invalid email format");
} else {
data.email = row.email.trim().toLowerCase();
if (existingEmails.has(data.email)) {
errors.push("Email already exists in database");
}
}

// Role validation
if (!row.role || !row.role.trim()) {
errors.push("Role is required");
} else if (!validateRole(row.role.trim())) {
errors.push(Invalid role. Must be one of: ${VALID_ROLES.join(", ")});
} else {
data.role = row.role.trim().toLowerCase();
}

// First name
if (!row.firstName || !row.firstName.trim()) {
errors.push("First name is required");
} else {
data.firstName = row.firstName.trim();
}

// Last name
if (!row.lastName || !row.lastName.trim()) {
errors.push("Last name is required");
} else {
data.lastName = row.lastName.trim();
}

// Phone (optional)
if (row.phoneNumber && row.phoneNumber.trim()) {
data.phoneNumber = row.phoneNumber.trim();
}

return {
isValid: errors.length === 0,
errors,
data,
};
};

/**

Validate bulk import - parse and validate without creating users

POST /api/v1/admin/onboarding/import/validate
*/
exports.validateImport = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
if (!req.file) {
return next(new AppError("CSV file is required", 400));
}

const rows = parseCSV(req.file.buffer);

if (rows.length === 0) {
return res.status(200).json({
status: "success",
data: {
totalRows: 0,
valid: 0,
invalid: 0,
validRows: [],
invalidRows: [],
},
});
}

// Get existing emails to detect duplicates
const existingUsers = await prisma.user.findMany({
where: { email: { in: rows.map((r) => r.email?.toLowerCase()).filter(Boolean) } },
select: { email: true },
});
const existingEmails = new Set(existingUsers.map((u) => u.email));

// Track duplicate emails within the import file
const seenEmails = new Set();
const validRows = [];
const invalidRows = [];

for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) {
const row = rows[i];
const rowNumber = i + 2; // +2 because row 1 is header

const validation = await validateRow(row, rowNumber, existingEmails);

if (!validation.isValid) {
  invalidRows.push({
    rowNumber,
    email: row.email || "N/A",
    errors: validation.errors,
  });
} else {
  // Check for duplicates within import
  if (seenEmails.has(validation.data.email)) {
    invalidRows.push({
      rowNumber,
      email: validation.data.email,
      errors: ["Duplicate email in import file"],
    });
  } else {
    seenEmails.add(validation.data.email);
    validRows.push({
      rowNumber,
      ...validation.data,
    });
  }
}

}

res.status(200).json({
status: "success",
data: {
totalRows: rows.length,
valid: validRows.length,
invalid: invalidRows.length,
validRows,
invalidRows,
},
});
});

/**

Create bulk import batch and users

POST /api/v1/admin/onboarding/import
*/
exports.createImport = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
if (!req.file) {
return next(new AppError("CSV file is required", 400));
}

const adminId = req.user.id;
const rows = parseCSV(req.file.buffer);

if (rows.length === 0) {
return next(new AppError("CSV file is empty", 400));
}

// Validate all rows first
const existingUsers = await prisma.user.findMany({
where: { email: { in: rows.map((r) => r.email?.toLowerCase()).filter(Boolean) } },
select: { email: true },
});
const existingEmails = new Set(existingUsers.map((u) => u.email));

const seenEmails = new Set();
const validRows = [];
const validationErrors = {};

for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) {
const row = rows[i];
const rowNumber = i + 2;

const validation = await validateRow(row, rowNumber, existingEmails);

if (!validation.isValid) {
  validationErrors[rowNumber] = validation.errors;
} else if (seenEmails.has(validation.data.email)) {
  validationErrors[rowNumber] = ["Duplicate email in import file"];
} else {
  seenEmails.add(validation.data.email);
  validRows.push({
    rowNumber,
    ...validation.data,
  });
}

}

if (validRows.length === 0) {
return res.status(400).json({
status: "fail",
data: {
message: "No valid rows to import",
validationErrors,
},
});
}

// Create batch and rows in transaction
const result = await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
// Create batch record
const batch = await tx.adminImportBatch.create({
data: {
adminId,
fileName: req.file.originalname,
totals: {
total: rows.length,
valid: validRows.length,
invalid: Object.keys(validationErrors).length,
},
},
});

const createdUsers = [];
const createdInvitations = [];
const failed = [];

// Create users and invitations
for (const rowData of validRows) {
  try {
    // Generate temp password
    const tempPassword = uuidv4();
    const hashedPassword = await bcrypt.hash(tempPassword, SALT_ROUNDS);

    // Generate claim token
    const { rawToken, hashedToken } = generateClaimToken();
    const expiresAt = new Date();
    expiresAt.setHours(expiresAt.getHours() + CLAIM_TOKEN_EXPIRY_HOURS);

    // Create user
    const user = await tx.user.create({
      data: {
        username: `${rowData.email.split("@")[0]}_${Date.now()}`,
        email: rowData.email,
        password: hashedPassword,
        role: rowData.role,
        phoneNumber: rowData.phoneNumber || null,
        isEmailVerified: false,
        onboardingStatus: "not_started",
      },
    });

    // Create invitation
    const invitation = await tx.userInvitation.create({
      data: {
        userId: user.id,
        adminId,
        tokenHash: hashedToken,
        expiresAt,
        status: "PENDING",
        batchId: batch.id,
      },
    });

    // Store raw token and user info for email sending (will be done after transaction)
    createdUsers.push({
      id: user.id,
      email: user.email,
      role: user.role,
      firstName: rowData.firstName,
      lastName: rowData.lastName,
      rawToken,
      invitationId: invitation.id,
    });

    // Log import row
    await tx.adminImportRow.create({
      data: {
        batchId: batch.id,
        rowNumber: rowData.rowNumber,
        email: rowData.email,
        payload: rowData,
        status: "SUCCESS",
      },
    });
  } catch (error) {
    failed.push({
      rowNumber: rowData.rowNumber,
      email: rowData.email,
      error: error.message,
    });
  }
}

// Log failed import rows
for (const [rowNumber, errors] of Object.entries(validationErrors)) {
  await tx.adminImportRow.create({
    data: {
      batchId: batch.id,
      rowNumber: parseInt(rowNumber),
      email: rows[parseInt(rowNumber) - 2]?.email || "N/A",
      payload: rows[parseInt(rowNumber) - 2] || {},
      status: "FAILED",
      errors,
    },
  });
}

// Audit log
await tx.auditLog.create({
  data: {
    adminId,
    action: "BULK_IMPORT_USERS",
    targetType: "AdminImportBatch",
    targetId: batch.id,
    metadata: {
      fileName: req.file.originalname,
      totalRows: rows.length,
      successCount: createdUsers.length,
      failCount: Object.keys(validationErrors).length,
    },
  },
});

return { batch, createdUsers, failed };

});

// Send invitation emails (outside transaction)
const emailResults = [];
for (const userData of result.createdUsers) {
try {
const claimUrl = ${getAppBaseUrl()}/claim-account?token=${userData.rawToken};
await sendEmail({
to: userData.email,
subject: "Claim Your Town Ruins Account",
html: buildBrandedEmail({
title: "Welcome to Town Ruins",
preheader: "Your administrator has created an account for you",
body: `

// Update invitation status to SENT
  await prisma.userInvitation.update({
    where: { id: userData.invitationId },
    data: { sentAt: new Date() },
  });
} catch (error) {
  emailResults.push({
    email: userData.email,
    status: "failed",
    error: error.message,
  });
}

}

auditLog.createEntry({
adminId,
action: "IMPORT_EMAILS_SENT",
targetType: "AdminImportBatch",
targetId: result.batch.id,
metadata: {
sentCount: emailResults.filter((r) => r.status === "sent").length,
failedCount: emailResults.filter((r) => r.status === "failed").length,
},
});

res.status(201).json({
status: "success",
data: {
batch: {
id: result.batch.id,
fileName: result.batch.fileName,
createdAt: result.batch.createdAt,
},
results: {
created: result.createdUsers.length,
failed: result.failed.length,
emailsSent: emailResults.filter((r) => r.status === "sent").length,
emailsFailed: emailResults.filter((r) => r.status === "failed").length,
},
failures: result.failed.length > 0 ? result.failed : null,
},
});
});

/**

Validate account claim token

GET /api/v1/account/claim/validate?token=...
*/
exports.validateClaimToken = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
const { token } = req.query;

if (!token) {
return next(new AppError("Claim token is required", 400));
}

const hashedToken = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(token).digest("hex");

const invitation = await prisma.userInvitation.findFirst({
where: {
tokenHash: hashedToken,
status: "PENDING",
},
include: {
user: {
select: {
id: true,
email: true,
role: true,
onboardingStatus: true,
},
},
},
});

if (!invitation) {
return next(new AppError("Invalid or expired claim token", 400));
}

if (invitation.expiresAt < new Date()) {
return next(new AppError("Claim token has expired", 400));
}

res.status(200).json({
status: "success",
data: {
user: invitation.user,
expiresAt: invitation.expiresAt,
},
});
});

/**

Claim account - set password and activate

POST /api/v1/account/claim
*/
exports.claimAccount = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
const { token, password, passwordConfirm } = req.body;

if (!token) {
return next(new AppError("Claim token is required", 400));
}

if (!password || !passwordConfirm) {
return next(new AppError("Password and confirmation are required", 400));
}

if (password !== passwordConfirm) {
return next(new AppError("Passwords do not match", 400));
}

if (password.length < 8) {
return next(new AppError("Password must be at least 8 characters", 400));
}

const hashedToken = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(token).digest("hex");

const invitation = await prisma.userInvitation.findFirst({
where: {
tokenHash: hashedToken,
status: "PENDING",
},
include: {
user: true,
},
});

if (!invitation) {
return next(new AppError("Invalid claim token", 400));
}

if (invitation.expiresAt < new Date()) {
return next(new AppError("Claim token has expired", 400));
}

if (invitation.claimedAt) {
return next(new AppError("This invitation has already been claimed", 400));
}

// Hash new password
const hashedPassword = await bcrypt.hash(password, SALT_ROUNDS);

// Update user and mark invitation as claimed
const user = await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
const updatedUser = await tx.user.update({
where: { id: invitation.userId },
data: {
password: hashedPassword,
isEmailVerified: true,
},
});

await tx.userInvitation.update({
  where: { id: invitation.id },
  data: {
    status: "CLAIMED",
    claimedAt: new Date(),
  },
});

// Audit log
await tx.auditLog.create({
  data: {
    adminId: invitation.adminId,
    action: "ACCOUNT_CLAIMED",
    targetType: "User",
    targetId: invitation.userId,
    metadata: {
      invitationId: invitation.id,
    },
  },
});

return updatedUser;

});

// Return JWT token for immediate authentication
const jwt = require("jsonwebtoken");
const authToken = jwt.sign({ id: user.id }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, {
expiresIn: process.env.JWT_EXPIRES_IN,
});

res.status(200).json({
status: "success",
token: authToken,
data: {
user: {
_id: user.id,
email: user.email,
username: user.username,
role: user.role,
onboardingStatus: user.onboardingStatus,
},
},
});
});

/**

Resend invitation email

POST /api/v1/admin/invitations/:invitationId/resend
*/
exports.resendInvitation = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
const { invitationId } = req.params;

const invitation = await prisma.userInvitation.findUnique({
where: { id: invitationId },
include: {
user: true,
},
});

if (!invitation) {
return next(new AppError("Invitation not found", 404));
}

if (invitation.status === "CLAIMED") {
return next(new AppError("Cannot resend invitation for already-claimed account", 400));
}

if (invitation.revokedAt) {
return next(new AppError("Invitation has been revoked", 400));
}

// Generate new token
const { rawToken, hashedToken } = generateClaimToken();
const expiresAt = new Date();
expiresAt.setHours(expiresAt.getHours() + CLAIM_TOKEN_EXPIRY_HOURS);

const updatedInvitation = await prisma.userInvitation.update({
where: { id: invitationId },
data: {
tokenHash: hashedToken,
expiresAt,
status: "PENDING",
sentAt: null,
},
});

// Send email
const claimUrl = ${getAppBaseUrl()}/claim-account?token=${rawToken};
try {
await sendEmail({
to: invitation.user.email,
subject: "Claim Your Town Ruins Account - Invitation Resent",
html: buildBrandedEmail({
title: "Welcome to Town Ruins",
preheader: "Resend: Claim your account",
body: `

await prisma.userInvitation.update({
  where: { id: invitationId },
  data: { sentAt: new Date() },
});

auditLog.createEntry({
  adminId: req.user.id,
  action: "INVITATION_RESENT",
  targetType: "UserInvitation",
  targetId: invitationId,
  metadata: {
    userId: invitation.userId,
    email: invitation.user.email,
  },
});

} catch (error) {
return next(
new AppError(
Could not resend invitation. Email error: ${error.message},
500
)
);
}

res.status(200).json({
status: "success",
data: {
message: "Invitation resent successfully",
invitation: {
id: updatedInvitation.id,
status: updatedInvitation.status,
expiresAt: updatedInvitation.expiresAt,
sentAt: updatedInvitation.sentAt,
},
},
});
});

/**

Revoke invitation

POST /api/v1/admin/invitations/:invitationId/revoke
*/
exports.revokeInvitation = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
const { invitationId } = req.params;

const invitation = await prisma.userInvitation.findUnique({
where: { id: invitationId },
});

if (!invitation) {
return next(new AppError("Invitation not found", 404));
}

if (invitation.claimedAt) {
return next(new AppError("Cannot revoke already-claimed invitation", 400));
}

if (invitation.revokedAt) {
return next(new AppError("Invitation already revoked", 400));
}

const revokedInvitation = await prisma.userInvitation.update({
where: { id: invitationId },
data: {
status: "REVOKED",
revokedAt: new Date(),
},
});

auditLog.createEntry({
adminId: req.user.id,
action: "INVITATION_REVOKED",
targetType: "UserInvitation",
targetId: invitationId,
metadata: {
userId: invitation.userId,
},
});

res.status(200).json({
status: "success",
data: {
message: "Invitation revoked",
invitation: revokedInvitation,
},
});
});

/**

Get pending invitations

GET /api/v1/admin/invitations?status=PENDING
*/
exports.getInvitations = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
const { status = "PENDING", page = 1, limit = 20 } = req.query;
const pageNum = Math.max(1, parseInt(page, 10) || 1);
const limitNum = Math.min(100, Math.max(1, parseInt(limit, 10) || 20));
const skip = (pageNum - 1) * limitNum;

const invitations = await prisma.UserInvitation.findMany({
where: status ? { status } : {},
include: {
user: {
select: {
id: true,
email: true,
username: true,
role: true,
},
},
admin: {
select: {
id: true,
email: true,
username: true,
},
},
},
orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" },
skip,
take: limitNum,
});

const total = await prisma.UserInvitation.count({
where: status ? { status } : {},
});

res.status(200).json({
status: "success",
data: {
invitations,
pagination: {
page: pageNum,
limit: limitNum,
total,
pages: Math.ceil(total / limitNum),
},
},
});
});

/**

Complete onboarding

POST /api/v1/account/onboarding/complete
*/
exports.completeOnboarding = catchAsync(async (req, res, next) => {
const userId = req.user.id;
const { skipped = false } = req.body;

const user = await prisma.user.update({
where: { id: userId },
data: {
onboardingStatus: skipped ? "skipped" : "completed",
onboardingCompletedAt: new Date(),
},
});

auditLog.createEntry({
adminId: userId,
action: "ONBOARDING_COMPLETED",
targetType: "User",
targetId: userId,
metadata: { skipped },
});

res.status(200).json({
status: "success",
data: {
user: {
_id: user.id,
onboardingStatus: user.onboardingStatus,
onboardingCompletedAt: user.onboardingCompletedAt,
},
},
});
});

});

Cost comparison

Your proposed architecture:

One EC2 instance

Docker containers

Local PostgreSQL

EBS volume for uploads

Security Groups

Typical monthly cost (outside Free Tier):

Service
Approx. cost
EC2
$6–20
EBS storage (50–100GB)
$4–10
Data transfer
depends on usage
Route53
~$0.50 per hosted zone
Total
~$10–30/month

Compared to:

Elastic Beanstalk

RDS PostgreSQL

S3

CloudFront

Load Balancer

which commonly ends up around $35–100+/month, with the load balancer and RDS being major contributors.

Running PostgreSQL locally

This is perfectly reasonable for:

MVP

Small production deployments

Hundreds of users

Thousands of listings

Advantages:

No RDS bill

Very fast local network access

Simple backups with pg_dump

Easy Docker Compose setup

The trade-off is that if the EC2 instance fails, your database goes down too. Regular backups become essential.

Storing images on EBS

Yes, you can store uploaded images directly on the instance's attached EBS volume, for example:

/srv/uploads

Pros:

No S3 costs

Very fast

Very simple

Cons:

If the instance is lost without snapshots, the images are lost.

Scaling to multiple application servers becomes difficult because only one instance has the files.

For an MVP, this is often an acceptable compromise.

One VPC

One VPC is the standard choice.

VPC
 ├── Public Subnet
 │     └── EC2
 │
 └── Security Group
       22 SSH
       80 HTTP
       443 HTTPS

There is no need to create separate VPCs for the frontend, backend, and database.

Docker Compose

A typical setup would be:

docker-compose.yml

nginx
frontend
backend
postgres

Nginx (or Caddy) routes traffic:

/
    → frontend

/api
    → backend

The backend connects to PostgreSQL over Docker's internal network.

What I'd recommend for Town Ruins

Given your current stage and cost sensitivity:

✅ One VPC

✅ One EC2 instance

✅ Docker Compose

✅ Frontend container

✅ Backend container

✅ PostgreSQL container

✅ EBS volume for uploads

✅ Automated nightly PostgreSQL backups

✅ Daily EBS snapshots

✅ Nginx or Caddy as the reverse proxy

✅ HTTPS with Let's Encrypt

Later, as usage grows, you can migrate incrementally:

Move uploads from EBS to S3.

Move PostgreSQL to RDS.

Add a second application instance.

Introduce a load balancer.

This path lets you keep initial costs low while leaving a straightforward migration path as Town Ruins grows.

Branding: Visitors first encounter a polished narrative about Town Ruins before entering the transactional experience.

Growth: It provides a natural place to add blog content, city guides, landlord resources, and announcements over time, helping build organic traffic.

No—these log entries are about two different connections, and it's easy to conflate them.

Database connection (working):

Connected to Aurora PostgreSQL

This is your backend server connecting from Elastic Beanstalk to Aurora over your VPC. It has nothing to do with the browser's Origin header.

CORS error (browser → backend):

CORS blocked for origin: http://98.90.30.184:80

This is Express inspecting the HTTP Origin header that the browser sent when calling your API. The database is not involved in this check.

If the browser sends:

Origin: http://98.90.30.184:80

then, at that moment, the browser believes the web page it's running came from http://98.90.30.184:80.

That does not mean your database IP is exposed.

The key question

What is 98.90.30.184?

If it's your Elastic Beanstalk public instance/load balancer IP, then someone (or something) accessed the frontend through that IP instead of https://app.townruins.com.

If it's your Aurora database endpoint/IP, then that would be a different concern—but Aurora endpoints are typically DNS names (e.g., *.rds.amazonaws.com), not raw public IPs, and private Aurora instances are not directly accessible from browsers.

How to verify

Run this from a terminal:

nslookup app.townruins.com
nslookup api.townruins.com

Then compare the resolved addresses with 98.90.30.184.

Also check:

curl -I http://98.90.30.184
curl -I https://app.townruins.com

If the IP serves your frontend, that explains the CORS origin.

If it doesn't, then we need to trace how the browser ended up using that origin.

Based on the log alone, I don't think this indicates your database connection is being exposed. It indicates the HTTP origin of the web application reaching your backend is unexpected. The next step is to identify exactly what service 98.90.30.184 belongs to.

## Response:
7/13/2026, 3:48:05 AM

That's actually a very useful clue.

If:

Visiting http://98.90.30.184 redirects to https://api.townruins.com, and

Your logs show Origin: http://98.90.30.184:80

then the request likely started on the IP address, not on api.townruins.com.

The important point is that the Origin header is set before the redirect. A redirect doesn't rewrite the browser's origin for that request.

This suggests one of these scenarios:

A client or bot is calling the API via the EB IP. This is common on public servers and generally harmless if your CORS policy rejects it.

Your frontend or another client is still configured to use the EB IP somewhere. For example, an old environment variable, hardcoded URL, or cached service worker.

Someone manually accessed the API using the IP, triggering the log.

What to determine next

You should find out whether your own frontend is generating these requests or whether they're coming from something external.

A good investigation would answer:

Does the log show a User-Agent like Chrome/Firefox (your frontend) or something like curl, python-requests, or a bot?

What endpoint was requested (/api/auth/login, /health, etc.)?

What was the Referer header, if any?

What is the source IP (req.ip or X-Forwarded-For)?

If the requests are from bots or scanners, your current behavior—rejecting them—is exactly what you want.

If they're from your frontend, then there's still a configuration issue to fix.

So at this point I would not add http://98.90.30.184 to your CORS allowlist. Instead, determine whether the requests originate from your application or from external traffic. If they're external, the CORS errors are evidence that your protection is working, not that it's broken.

This is not an invalid token error. It is a missing endpoint (404).

Your email probably contains something like

https://api.townruins.com/verify-email?token=...

https://app.townruins.com/verify-email?token=...

verify-email

router.get("/verify-email", verifyEmail);

Many Express apps mount routes like

app.use("/api/auth", authRoutes);

and inside

router.get("/verify-email", ...)

/api/auth/verify-email

/verify-email

depending on your API.

Repository Invariant

Any implementation, documentation, API, UI, or test that contradicts these rules is considered a repository defect and must be corrected.

This gives Traycer a single source of truth it can enforce whenever it audits or modifies the repository.

Listing Updated
    ↓
Kafka/SQS/Event Bus
    ↓
Syndication Workers
    ↓
Destination Adapters
    ↓
Rate Limited Delivery

Never sync directly from request lifecycle.

Destination Adapter Pattern

Each platform gets its own adapter.

interface SyndicationAdapter {
  validate(listing)
  transform(listing)
  publish(payload)
  update(remoteId, payload)
  remove(remoteId)
  syncStatus()
}

Examples:

AirbnbAdapter

FacebookMarketplaceAdapter

GoogleVacationRentalAdapter

This prevents platform-specific chaos leaking into core business logic.

Critical Features

1. Selective Syndication

[x] Facebook

3. Conflict Resolution

## Response:
5/21/2026, 10:50:52 PM

Your backend is either:

not responding correctly to OPTIONS preflight requests, or

not returning CORS headers on error responses / proxied responses.

Since all requests from https://app.townruins.com → https://api.townruins.com are failing, this is almost certainly a global API gateway / reverse proxy / Express/NestJS CORS config issue.

The important part:

No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present

That means the browser never received a valid CORS response from the API.

Immediate Checks

1. Verify API is actually reachable

Run:

curl -I https://api.townruins.com/health

and:

curl -X OPTIONS https://api.townruins.com/api/v1/listings/home/highlighted \
  -H "Origin: https://app.townruins.com" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: GET"

You should see headers like:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.townruins.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE,OPTIONS
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization

If not, backend/proxy config is broken.

Correct Backend Fix

Express

import cors from 'cors'

app.use(cors({
  origin: [
    'https://app.townruins.com',
    'http://localhost:3000'
  ],
  credentials: true,
}))

app.options('*', cors())

NestJS

Main bootstrap:

app.enableCors({
  origin: [
    'https://app.townruins.com',
    'http://localhost:3000',
  ],
  credentials: true,
  methods: 'GET,HEAD,PUT,PATCH,POST,DELETE,OPTIONS',
  allowedHeaders: [
    'Content-Type',
    'Authorization',
    'Accept',
  ],
})

If Using NGINX

This is VERY commonly the actual problem.

Add:

location / {
    proxy_pass http://localhost:5000;

    add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin https://app.townruins.com always;
    add_header Access-Control-Allow-Credentials true always;
    add_header Access-Control-Allow-Methods "GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS" always;
    add_header Access-Control-Allow-Headers "Authorization, Content-Type" always;

    if ($request_method = OPTIONS) {
        return 204;
    }
}

The always keyword matters because without it, headers disappear on 4xx/5xx responses.

Cloudflare / Reverse Proxy Possibility

If the API is behind:

Cloudflare

Traefik

AWS ALB

API Gateway

Caddy

then the proxy layer may be stripping headers or intercepting OPTIONS.

Especially if:

backend works locally

production suddenly broke

direct IP works

Very Likely Root Cause

Given your architecture, I strongly suspect one of these:

A. Backend crashed

The proxy returns HTML/502 without CORS headers.

Check:

pm2 logs

or:

docker logs <container>

B. New auth middleware intercepts OPTIONS

This breaks preflight:

app.use(authMiddleware)

before CORS middleware.

CORS MUST be first.

Correct order:

app.use(cors())
app.use(express.json())
app.use(authMiddleware)

C. NGINX forwarding issue

Common mistake:

proxy_pass http://localhost:5000/api;

causing route mismatch and internal 404s without CORS headers.

Production-Grade Recommendation

Do not manually manage headers everywhere.

Centralize CORS:

Backend

const allowedOrigins = [
  'https://app.townruins.com',
  'http://localhost:3000',
]

app.enableCors({
  origin(origin, callback) {
    if (!origin || allowedOrigins.includes(origin)) {
      callback(null, true)
    } else {
      callback(new Error('Not allowed by CORS'))
    }
  },
  credentials: true,
})

Also Check This

If frontend sends:

credentials: 'include'

then backend CANNOT use:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

It must be the exact domain.

Fastest Debug Path

SSH into production and run:

curl -i https://api.townruins.com/api/v1/listings/home/highlighted

then:

curl -i -X OPTIONS \
  https://api.townruins.com/api/v1/listings/home/highlighted \
  -H "Origin: https://app.townruins.com" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: GET"

That will immediately reveal whether:

backend is down

proxy is swallowing headers

OPTIONS unsupported

CORS misconfigured

auth middleware blocking preflight

## Response:
5/22/2026, 2:15:35 AM

Your Prisma schema does not have a deletedAt field on the Room model, but your query is trying to filter on it.

This line is the problem:

deletedAt: null,

inside:

prisma.room.count({
  where: {
    status: "AVAILABLE",
    deletedAt: null,

Prisma is telling you:

Unknown argument deletedAt

meaning the generated Prisma client for Room has no such column.

Immediate Fix

Remove:

deletedAt: null,

from all Room queries.

So change:

where: {
  status: "AVAILABLE",
  deletedAt: null,
  accommodation: {

to:

where: {
  status: "AVAILABLE",
  accommodation: {

Why This Happened

You probably:

added soft deletes to Accommodation

copied filters into Room

but never added deletedAt to the Prisma Room model

You CAN still filter nested accommodation soft deletion:

accommodation: {
  is: {
    deletedAt: null
  }
}

That part is valid because Accommodation likely has deletedAt.

Proper Long-Term Fix Options

Option A — No Room Soft Delete (simplest)

Just remove all:

deletedAt: null

from:

prisma.room.findMany

prisma.room.count

RoomWhereInput

This is probably what you want.

Option B — Add Soft Deletes to Room

If rooms should support deletion independently:

Prisma schema

model Room {
  id         String   @id @default(cuid())
  deletedAt  DateTime?
}

Then:

npx prisma migrate dev -n add-room-soft-delete
npx prisma generate

or production:

npx prisma migrate deploy
npx prisma generate

Another Important Issue In Your Query

This:

select: {
  _count: {
    select: {
      _all: true
    }
  }
}

inside count() is also invalid Prisma usage.

count() does NOT use select.

Correct:

const roomTotal = await prisma.room.count({
  where: {
    status: "AVAILABLE",
    accommodation: {
      is: {
        verificationStatus: "APPROVED",
        isPublished: true,
        deletedAt: null,
      },
    },
    capacity: {
      gte: 1,
    },
  },
})

Your Query Should Probably Become

const [roomTotal, rooms] = await Promise.all([
  prisma.room.count({
    where: {
      status: "AVAILABLE",
      accommodation: {
        is: {
          verificationStatus: "APPROVED",
          isPublished: true,
          deletedAt: null,
        },
      },
      capacity: {
        gte: 1,
      },
    },
  }),

  prisma.room.findMany({
    where: {
      status: "AVAILABLE",
      accommodation: {
        is: {
          verificationStatus: "APPROVED",
          isPublished: true,
          deletedAt: null,
        },
      },
      capacity: {
        gte: 1,
      },
    },
  }),
])

Why This Broke Production

Prisma validates queries at runtime.

Once execution reaches that branch:

prisma.room.count()

it throws before SQL execution.

If this endpoint powers homepage listings, the request crashes → proxy returns 500 → browser reports CORS failure because error response lacks CORS headers.

So your earlier "CORS issue" was likely actually a backend exception.

React Example

import { signInWithPopup } from 'firebase/auth'
import { auth, googleProvider } from '@/lib/firebase'

async function loginWithGoogle() {
  const result = await signInWithPopup(auth, googleProvider)

  const firebaseToken = await result.user.getIdToken()

  const response = await fetch(
    'https://api.townruins.com/api/v1/auth/firebase',
    {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      },
      credentials: 'include',
      body: JSON.stringify({
        token: firebaseToken,
      }),
    }
  )

  const data = await response.json()

  localStorage.setItem('accessToken', data.accessToken)
}

12. Verify Firebase Token

Auth Controller

import admin from '../firebaseAdmin'

export async function firebaseLogin(req, res) {
  try {
    const { token } = req.body

    if (!token) {
      return res.status(400).json({
        error: 'Missing token',
      })
    }

    const decoded = await admin.auth().verifyIdToken(token)

    const {
      uid,
      email,
      name,
      picture,
    } = decoded

    let user = await prisma.user.findUnique({
      where: { email },
    })

    if (!user) {
      user = await prisma.user.create({
        data: {
          email,
          name,
          avatarUrl: picture,
          firebaseUid: uid,
          authProvider: 'GOOGLE',
          emailVerified: true,
        },
      })
    }

    const accessToken = generateJwt(user)

    return res.json({
      accessToken,
      user,
    })
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error)

    return res.status(401).json({
      error: 'Invalid Firebase token',
    })
  }
}

Yes — I checked the current main branch of hwevaproduction-debug/towruins, and your concern is valid.

What the current system has

The user model already has the infrastructure for password recovery:

passwordResetToken

passwordResetExpires

email verification token fields

The current user routes also expose:

POST /signup

POST /login

email verification

phone verification

POST /forgot-password

POST /reset-password

and then authenticated user update/delete routes.

So password recovery exists, but that is not the same thing as securely changing an existing password.

The important security gap

For an authenticated user changing their password, the system should not simply accept a new password through the generic user update endpoint.

The correct flow should be:

User opens Change Password.

User enters:

Current password

New password

Confirm new password

Backend authenticates the request.

Backend verifies the current password with bcrypt.

Backend validates the new password.

Backend prevents the new password from being identical to the old one.

Backend hashes the new password with bcrypt.

Backend changes the password atomically.

Existing authentication sessions/tokens are invalidated or rotated.

User receives a password-changed notification by email.

User also receives an in-app security notification.

Ideally, the notification tells them what to do if they did not make the change.

The repository already has a fairly mature notification infrastructure: it supports email, SMS, in-app and push delivery, with user notification preferences and queued notification jobs.

The worker subsequently processes those jobs through the appropriate channel and retries failures.

The other issue I found

The notification event registry currently contains things such as:

booking events

provider approval/rejection/suspension

accommodation events

dispute resolution

report resolution

but there is no password-security event.

Likewise, the notification template registry only loads the booking and provider template collections.

So we should add a dedicated security event rather than hacking password-change messaging into an unrelated notification.

What I recommend implementing

I'd make this a proper security feature rather than just modifying the existing /update/:id.

Backend

Add:

POST /api/v1/users/change-password

Request:

{
  "currentPassword": "old-password",
  "newPassword": "new-password",
  "confirmPassword": "new-password"
}

The endpoint should require protect.

It should never accept a user ID from the client for identifying whose password is being changed. It should use:

req.user.id

That avoids the possibility of someone attempting to change another user's password through an ID manipulation attack.

Password verification

Use the existing bcrypt/password utility:

comparePassword(currentPassword, user.password)

The repository already imports comparePassword in authController.

If the current password is wrong:

401 Incorrect current password

Do not reveal whether any other account information is valid.

Password reset

Keep the existing:

forgot-password
reset-password

flow separate.

That is important because:

Change password
→ user is authenticated
→ must prove current password

Forgot password
→ user cannot prove current password
→ possession of the verified reset link/token proves account control

The reset token should remain single-use and expire quickly.

Notification

I'd introduce:

security.password_changed

with:

Email

Your Town Ruins password was changed successfully.

Include:

account identifier/email

timestamp

security warning

"If you did not make this change, contact support immediately."

In-app

Password changed
Your Town Ruins password was successfully changed.

And if push is enabled, the existing notification infrastructure can deliver it automatically.

The existing notification service already handles user preferences and generates email/in-app/push jobs, so we don't need to create another notification mechanism.

One more thing I would change

I would not stop at the notification.

A password change should invalidate existing sessions.

Your application currently uses JWT authentication. That means simply changing the database password does not necessarily invalidate an already-issued JWT.

So if someone has stolen a user's JWT, changing the password could leave that stolen token usable until its normal expiration.

A proper production implementation should add something like:

passwordChangedAt

to User.

Then JWT validation can reject tokens issued before that timestamp.

For example:

passwordChangedAt = 2026-08-20 14:20:00

and a token issued at:

2026-08-20 13:00:00

becomes invalid.

This is particularly important because the system is now being prepared for production.

Recommended final security model

Action
Verification
Notification
Sessions
Change password
Current password
Email + in-app + push
Invalidate old tokens
Forgot password
Reset token sent to email
Email
Invalidate old tokens
Reset password
Valid reset token
Email + in-app
Invalidate old tokens
Admin-forced password reset
Admin authorization + reset mechanism
Email + in-app
Invalidate old tokens

I would implement all three pieces together: change-password + password-change notification + token/session invalidation. That gives Town Ruins a proper account-security workflow rather than merely adding another password field to the existing user update API.

Inspecting Room Listing Routes and Controllers

Worked for 41s

I checked the current main repo and the code you pasted. The problem is not primarily the <img> element. It is an image-data contract mismatch between the upload/storage side, the room API, and StayCard.

What is happening

Your StayCard currently resolves the image like this:

if (Array.isArray(room?.images) && room.images.length > 0) {
  const firstImage = room.images[0];
  return typeof firstImage === "string"
    ? firstImage
    : firstImage?.url || FALLBACK_IMAGE;
}

if (typeof room?.image === "string") return room.image;
if (typeof room?.coverImage === "string") return room.coverImage;

return FALLBACK_IMAGE;

So the card only knows about:

room.images

room.image

room.coverImage

But the backend has two separate image systems:

AccommodationImage

RoomImage

The Prisma schema explicitly makes Room.images a relation to RoomImage, while Accommodation.images is a separate relation to AccommodationImage.

More importantly: the public room API transforms the images

The backend's decoratePublicRoom() does this:

images: (room.images || []).map((image) => image.url).filter(Boolean),
coverImage: room.images?.[0]?.url || null,

So when you hit GET /rooms/:id, the expected result is:

{
  "images": [
    "https://..."
  ],
  "coverImage": "https://..."
}

not:

{
  "images": [
    {
      "id": "...",
      "url": "https://..."
    }
  ]
}

The backend is deliberately flattening RoomImage objects to URL strings for the public room response.

The likely actual failure

The upload endpoint itself is correctly storing a room image:

exports.addRoomImage = ...

and creates:

{
  roomId,
  url,
  altText,
  isCover,
  sortOrder
}

in RoomImage.

So if the user uploads an image successfully, the database can contain it.

The issue is likely the endpoint supplying the collection of rooms to the page containing StayCard is not returning those RoomImage records in the shape that StayCard expects.

That's why this is important:

If room.images is absent/empty at the point where StayCard renders, your code has no choice but to return FALLBACK_IMAGE.

The fallback isn't detecting a broken image. It's detecting missing image data.

There is also an architectural clue

The backend has:

Accommodation
 ├── images → AccommodationImage
 └── rooms
       └── images → RoomImage

But your card represents a room/stay, not an accommodation.

Therefore, the correct image priority should be something like:

room.images
↓
room.coverImage
↓
room.accommodation.images
↓
room.accommodation.coverImage
↓
fallback

Right now your card never checks room.accommodation.images.

That is a significant gap because the backend's accommodation API explicitly returns accommodation images, while the room API has its own room images.

So I would fix it in two places

1. Make StayCard resilient to both room and accommodation images.

Something along these lines:

const getRoomImage = (room: any) => {
  const roomImages = room?.images;

  if (Array.isArray(roomImages) && roomImages.length > 0) {
    const first = roomImages[0];

    if (typeof first === "string" && first.trim()) {
      return first;
    }

    if (first?.url) {
      return first.url;
    }
  }

  if (typeof room?.coverImage === "string" && room.coverImage.trim()) {
    return room.coverImage;
  }

  const accommodationImages = room?.accommodation?.images;

  if (Array.isArray(accommodationImages) && accommodationImages.length > 0) {
    const first = accommodationImages[0];

    if (typeof first === "string" && first.trim()) {
      return first;
    }

    if (first?.url) {
      return first.url;
    }
  }

  if (
    typeof room?.accommodation?.coverImage === "string" &&
    room.accommodation.coverImage.trim()
  ) {
    return room.accommodation.coverImage;
  }

  if (typeof room?.image === "string" && room.image.trim()) {
    return room.image;
  }

  return FALLBACK_IMAGE;
};

2. More importantly, fix the API feeding the StayCard.

I would not rely on the card to compensate for an incomplete API response.

The public temporary-stay listing endpoint should return every room with at least:

{
  "images": ["https://..."],
  "coverImage": "https://..."
}

for the room itself.

The backend already has the correct transformation logic in decoratePublicRoom().

So the next thing I would trace is:

Upload image
    ↓
RoomImage
    ↓
room listing/search endpoint
    ↓
Redux/API response
    ↓
StayCard.room
    ↓
getRoomImage()

I strongly suspect the break is between RoomImage and the endpoint that populates the StayCard, rather than the upload itself.

One other important point: the repo's current main branch does not appear to contain the exact StayCard you pasted-the repository metadata is current through August 18, while your pasted component appears to be from a newer/local frontend state. So I would not blindly modify the GitHub main card based only on this snippet.

If you want, I can trace the entire temporary-stay flow in the repo—from image upload → database → API → frontend query → StayCard—and identify the exact line where the image disappears.

Yes. Since you want one terminal command, use this. It updates StayCard so uploaded room images, accommodation images, object-form images, and coverImage are all handled before falling back.

replacement = '''const getRoomImage = (room: any) => {
  const resolveImage = (image: any) => {
    if (typeof image === "string" && image.trim()) return image;
    if (image?.url && typeof image.url === "string" && image.url.trim()) return image.url;
    return null;
  };

  const roomImages = Array.isArray(room?.images) ? room.images : [];
  const accommodationImages = Array.isArray(room?.accommodation?.images)
    ? room.accommodation.images
    : [];

  const image =
    roomImages.map(resolveImage).find(Boolean) ||
    resolveImage(room?.coverImage) ||
    accommodationImages.map(resolveImage).find(Boolean) ||
    resolveImage(room?.accommodation?.coverImage) ||
    resolveImage(room?.image);

  return image || FALLBACK_IMAGE;
};'''

accommodation.coverImage: "https://..."

The fallback isn't detecting a broken image. It's detecting missing image data.

There is also an architectural clue

The backend has:

Accommodation
 ├── images → AccommodationImage
 └── rooms
       └── images → RoomImage

But your card represents a room/stay, not an accommodation.

Therefore, the correct image priority should be something like:

room.images
↓
room.coverImage
↓
room.accommodation.images
↓
room.accommodation.coverImage
↓
fallback

Right now your card never checks room.accommodation.images.

That is a significant gap because the backend's accommodation API explicitly returns accommodation images, while the room API has its own room images.

So I would fix it in two places

1. Make StayCard resilient to both room and accommodation images.

Something along these lines:

const getRoomImage = (room: any) => {
  const roomImages = room?.images;

  if (Array.isArray(roomImages) && roomImages.length > 0) {
    const first = roomImages[0];

    if (typeof first === "string" && first.trim()) {
      return first;
    }

    if (first?.url) {
      return first.url;
    }
  }

  if (typeof room?.coverImage === "string" && room.coverImage.trim()) {
    return room.coverImage;
  }

  const accommodationImages = room?.accommodation?.images;

  if (Array.isArray(accommodationImages) && accommodationImages.length > 0) {
    const first = accommodationImages[0];

    if (typeof first === "string" && first.trim()) {
      return first;
    }

    if (first?.url) {
      return first.url;
    }
  }

  if (
    typeof room?.accommodation?.coverImage === "string" &&
    room.accommodation.coverImage.trim()
  ) {
    return room.accommodation.coverImage;
  }

  if (typeof room?.image === "string" && room.image.trim()) {
    return room.image;
  }

  return FALLBACK_IMAGE;
};

2. More importantly, fix the API feeding the StayCard.

I would not rely on the card to compensate for an incomplete API response.

The public temporary-stay listing endpoint should return every room with at least:

{
  "images": ["https://..."],
  "coverImage": "https://..."
}

for the room itself.

The backend already has the correct transformation logic in decoratePublicRoom().

So the next thing I would trace is:

Upload image
    ↓
RoomImage
    ↓
room listing/search endpoint
    ↓
Redux/API response
    ↓
StayCard.room
    ↓
getRoomImage()

I strongly suspect the break is between RoomImage and the endpoint that populates the StayCard, rather than the upload itself.

So I would not blindly modify the GitHub main card based only on this snippet.

If you want, I can trace the entire temporary-stay flow in the repo—from image upload → database → API → frontend query → StayCard—and identify the exact line where the image disappears.

how clear is the concept of friction of distance maps by james c scott

Response:

8/21/2026, 8:46:04 AM

If you mean James C. Scott’s idea of “friction of distance” in Seeing Like a State, I’d say the concept is quite clear once you separate it from the ordinary geographic meaning of distance.

Scott’s basic point is:

Distance creates friction because moving people, goods, information, and administrative authority across space takes time, money, effort, and knowledge.

So a map can make a territory look easy to govern without showing the actual difficulty of reaching and controlling what is on the ground.

The key distinction

Imagine a government has a map showing:

Capital → District A → Village B

On the map, Village B might be only 50 km away.

But in reality:

there may be no usable road;

rivers may be difficult to cross;

terrain may be mountainous;

information may travel slowly;

officials may not speak the local language;

local communities may resist outside authority;

seasonal conditions may make the route impassable.

So 50 km on the map ≠ 50 km of administrative accessibility.

That's where Scott's broader argument becomes important. States often try to make society “legible”—turning complicated local realities into standardized categories that can be seen and managed from the center. Maps are one of the major tools for doing this.

Why the concept matters

Scott is essentially challenging the assumption that geometric space is the same as lived space.

A conventional map tends to represent:

distance → measurable in kilometers

Scott is interested in something closer to:

distance → cost/friction of actually traversing or governing that space

You could therefore think of it as:

Effective distance = geographic distance + the obstacles to movement, communication, and control.

It's not necessarily a formal mathematical equation in Scott; it's a useful way of understanding the argument.

Where it gets especially interesting

The concept becomes powerful when applied to state-building.

A centralized state might draw administrative boundaries and create a standardized map of its territory. From the center, everything appears neatly organized:

State → province → district → village

But the state's actual ability to exercise authority diminishes as the friction of distance increases.

This helps explain why states historically invested in:

roads

railways

cadastral surveys

standardized place names

population censuses

postal systems

telecommunications

administrative centers

These technologies don't merely help people move. They reduce the friction between the center and the periphery.

So, for Scott, infrastructure can be understood partly as a way of compressing administrative distance.

One important qualification

If you're asking specifically about a “Friction of Distance Map by James C. Scott,” I would want to see the particular map/figure you're referring to, because Scott discusses legibility, mapping, spatial organization, and state capacity in several contexts, and “friction of distance” is also a broader concept in geography.

If you upload the map or tell me the book/chapter/page where you found it, I can explain exactly what every element of that map is showing and how Scott's argument works through it.

→ feedback / revenue

So recruitment is actually upstream of your development capacity.

If you need another developer but recruiting takes six weeks to find one, that's organizational friction of distance.

Your biggest advantage is that you can keep the map very short

I wouldn't recommend introducing layers just because you're thinking about SDLC administration.

You probably want something closer to:

Business

CEO(s)

↓

Technical execution

Developer 1 ↔ Developer 2

↓

Controlled environments

↓

That's enough.

The administrative system should make this path visible, not add managers to it.

I'd introduce only a few formal mechanisms

For an operation of this size, I'd want five things.

Single prioritized backlog

Every request goes into one system.

Not:

"CEO A told me on WhatsApp."

Not:

"CEO B mentioned it yesterday."

Everything becomes a traceable task.

Explicit priority authority

The two CEOs need a rule for resolving competing priorities.

For example:

Business priority is jointly determined by CEOs.

Developers determine technical implementation, not business priority.

That distinction is extremely important.

Technical ownership

Every major subsystem has an owner.

For example:

The exact assignment doesn't matter as much as unambiguous ownership.

Production change traceability

Every production change should answer:

What changed?
Why?
Who changed it?
Was it tested?

That's your administrative "map."

Incident feedback loop

When something breaks:

Production

→ incident

→ diagnosis

→ fix

→ deployment

→ verification

→ root cause

→ backlog item

→ prevention

Otherwise the organization repeatedly travels through the same friction.

The really interesting conclusion

With 2 CEOs + 2 developers + recruiters, Town Ruins doesn't have a bureaucracy problem.

It has the opposite potential problem:

The organization is so small that its administrative structure can become invisible.

And that is where Scott's idea becomes very useful.

You don't need a huge management apparatus.

You need legibility without bureaucracy.

The organization should be small enough that:

CEO → developer → production

can remain extremely short,

while documentation, ownership, environments, issue tracking, and monitoring ensure that the short distance doesn't turn into ambiguity.

In other words:

Don't increase organizational distance to create control. Create legibility and explicit ownership to create control.

For a four-person core operation, I'd consider that the central SDLC administration principle.

## Prompt:
8/21/2026, 8:46:15 AM

how clear is the concept of friction of distance maps by james c scott

## Response:
8/21/2026, 8:46:04 AM

If you mean James C. Scott’s idea of “friction of distance” in Seeing Like a State, I’d say the concept is quite clear once you separate it from the ordinary geographic meaning of distance.

Scott’s basic point is:

Distance creates friction because moving people, goods, information, and administrative authority across space takes time, money, effort, and knowledge.

So a map can make a territory look easy to govern without showing the actual difficulty of reaching and controlling what is on the ground.

The key distinction

Imagine a government has a map showing:

Capital → District A → Village B

On the map, Village B might be only 50 km away.

But in reality:

there may be no usable road;

rivers may be difficult to cross;

terrain may be mountainous;

information may travel slowly;

officials may not speak the local language;

local communities may resist outside authority;

seasonal conditions may make the route impassable.

So 50 km on the map ≠ 50 km of administrative accessibility.

That's where Scott's broader argument becomes important. States often try to make society “legible”—turning complicated local realities into standardized categories that can be seen and managed from the center. Maps are one of the major tools for doing this.

Why the concept matters

Scott is essentially challenging the assumption that geometric space is the same as lived space.

A conventional map tends to represent:

distance → measurable in kilometers

Scott is interested in something closer to:

distance → cost/friction of actually traversing or governing that space

You could therefore think of it as:

Effective distance = geographic distance + the obstacles to movement, communication, and control.

It's not necessarily a formal mathematical equation in Scott; it's a useful way of understanding the argument.

Where it gets especially interesting

The concept becomes powerful when applied to state-building.

A centralized state might draw administrative boundaries and create a standardized map of its territory. From the center, everything appears neatly organized:

State → province → district → village

But the state's actual ability to exercise authority diminishes as the friction of distance increases.

This helps explain why states historically invested in:

roads

railways

cadastral surveys

standardized place names

population censuses

postal systems

telecommunications

administrative centers

These technologies don't merely help people move. They reduce the friction between the center and the periphery.

So, for Scott, infrastructure can be understood partly as a way of compressing administrative distance.

One important qualification

If you're asking specifically about a “Friction of Distance Map by James C. Scott,” I would want to see the particular map/figure you're referring to, because Scott discusses legibility, mapping, spatial organization, and state capacity in several contexts, and “friction of distance” is also a broader concept in geography.

If you upload the map or tell me the book/chapter/page where you found it, I can explain exactly what every element of that map is showing and how Scott's argument works through it.

Yes. Applied to Town Ruins, Scott’s idea becomes surprisingly useful—not as a geographic theory, but as a way of thinking about organizational and SDLC distance.

The central translation would be:

In an SDLC, “friction of distance” is the cost, delay, uncertainty, and loss of control created when information, decisions, code, responsibilities, and business requirements have to travel between different parts of the organization and system.

For Town Ruins, this gives you a useful framework for understanding why some changes are easy to implement while others become disproportionately difficult.

1. The Town Ruins equivalent of “distance”

Consider the path:

Business requirement → product decision → development → code → testing → staging → production → monitoring → business outcome

There may be no physical distance involved, but there is organizational distance.

For example:

Business owner identifies a password-security problem
↓
Requirement is communicated
↓
Developer interprets requirement
↓
Developer changes backend
↓
Frontend must be changed
↓
Database may need migration
↓
Email/notification system must change
↓
Staging is tested
↓
Production deployment occurs
↓
Logs are monitored
↓
Business confirms the feature works

Every arrow introduces potential friction.

The farther a requirement has to travel before becoming an observable business result, the greater the opportunity for:

misunderstanding;

delay;

duplicated work;

inconsistent implementation;

loss of context;

responsibility gaps;

deployment errors;

business requirements becoming detached from the actual software.

2. Your architecture already demonstrates this

Town Ruins isn't simply:

Frontend → Backend → Database

Operationally it is closer to:

Users

↓

Frontend

↓

Nginx / CloudFront / routing

↓

Backend API

↓

Prisma / database

↓

Email / notifications / storage / payments

↓

background workers / cron jobs

↓

AWS / Docker / infrastructure

↓

operations

↓

business processes

Each additional boundary creates potential friction.

For example, when you encountered:

PUT /api/v1/users/update/undefined

the problem wasn't necessarily that updating a user is technically complicated.

The problem was distance between two representations of the same business operation:

Frontend:

updateProfile({ id, payload })

Backend API layer:

expected flattened parameters.

The business concept was simply:

“Update this user's profile.”

But the implementation had multiple representations of that concept.

That is friction.

3. SDLC administration is essentially the management of friction

This is where Scott's concept becomes particularly useful.

An SDLC administrator is not merely managing programmers.

They are managing the movement of information and control through the development system.

You can therefore conceptualize your SDLC like this:

SDLC element
Friction
Business → Product
Requirement ambiguity
Product → Developer
Specification loss
Developer → Repository
Implementation complexity
Repository → CI
Build/configuration friction
CI → Staging
Deployment friction
Staging → Production
Release friction
Production → Operations
Observability friction
Operations → Business
Feedback friction

The administration objective becomes:

Reduce unnecessary friction while preserving necessary control.

That last part is important.

You don't want to eliminate every boundary.

You want controlled boundaries.

4. Your staging environment is an excellent example

You recently created a separate staging environment.

From a purely technical perspective, that introduces additional infrastructure:

Production

and

Staging

instead of one environment.

That appears to increase distance.

But administratively it actually reduces a more dangerous form of friction:

the distance between development and safe production validation.

Without staging:

Developer → Production

With staging:

Developer → Staging → Production

You've added one step, but you've reduced:

production risk;

uncertainty;

rollback pressure;

testing ambiguity;

business disruption.

So Scott's framework shouldn't be interpreted as:

“fewer steps are always better.”

Rather:

The objective is to minimize costly friction, not necessarily the number of organizational boundaries.

A staging environment is a productive friction.

5. Your production/staging separation also creates “legibility”

This is where Scott's concept of legibility becomes extremely relevant.

A business needs to know:

What version is running?

Where is it running?

What database does it use?

Which environment is this?

Who owns the change?

What changed?

Was it tested?

Is the system healthy?

What happens if it fails?

If those things aren't clearly represented, the system becomes difficult to govern.

That is essentially an SDLC version of Scott's argument:

A system that cannot be easily represented, categorized and observed is difficult to administer.

Your move toward:

production vs staging;

Docker Compose configurations;

environment files;

deployment procedures;

runbooks;

monitoring;

changelogs;

migration reports;

implementation plans;

is therefore not merely “documentation.”

It is an attempt to make the software organization legible.

6. The business side has exactly the same problem

Take a Town Ruins booking.

The business concept is simple:

Tenant wants to book accommodation.

But operationally that may cross:

Tenant

→ listing

→ landlord

→ booking request

→ availability

→ payment

→ token/payment rules

→ notification

→ accommodation records

→ booking status

→ reminder jobs

→ reconciliation

→ financial records

→ business reporting

The business sees one transaction.

The system sees many subsystems.

That difference is a major source of friction.

And this is one of the most important applications of the concept to Town Ruins:

The more technical distance exists between a business event and the system's representation of that event, the harder the platform becomes to administer.

7. Consider your notification system

Suppose the business rule is:

“When something important happens to a user's account, the user must be notified.”

That sounds trivial.

But implementation might involve:

User action

→ backend event

→ database change

→ notification creation

→ notification worker

→ email service

→ SMTP/SES

→ delivery

→ user

Now imagine the user says:

“I changed my password but didn't receive anything.”

Where is the problem?

It could be:

frontend;

API;

authentication logic;

database;

notification creation;

worker;

SMTP;

email provider;

delivery.

The business event is one thing.

The technical path is many things.

That is friction of distance.

8. This also explains why debugging Town Ruins can feel disproportionately difficult

A bug isn't necessarily difficult because the code itself is difficult.

It can be difficult because the distance between symptom and cause is large.

For example:

User sees 404

↓

Frontend route?

↓

Nginx?

↓

Backend route?

↓

Controller?

↓

Database?

↓

Environment variable?

↓

Wrong deployment?

The symptom may occur at one end of the system while the cause exists somewhere completely different.

So an important SDLC administration metric could be:

Mean Diagnostic Distance

Conceptually:

How many organizational/system boundaries must be crossed before the cause of an incident can be identified?

The greater this distance, the greater the operational cost.

9. Your user deletion incident illustrates another form of friction

You had a user that couldn't simply be deleted because other entities referenced that user.

The business operation was:

Delete user.

The actual system relationship was:

User

→ Accommodation

→ Notifications

→ Notification jobs

→ Wallet transactions

→ other dependent records

So the database's relational structure created structural friction.

This isn't necessarily bad.

In fact, foreign-key constraints are protective friction.

They prevent administrators from casually destroying related business data.

But the administration problem becomes:

Does the administrator understand the dependency map?

If not, the database becomes difficult to govern.

Your SQL investigation into referencing tables was effectively an attempt to make the dependency structure legible.

10. From a business perspective, friction can become money

This is probably the most important business application.

Suppose:

Business requirement → production feature

normally takes:

2 days

but because of organizational/technical friction it takes:

8 days.

The additional six days aren't just a developer inconvenience.

They represent:

delayed revenue;

delayed customer acquisition;

delayed security improvements;

delayed operational improvements;

opportunity cost;

management overhead.

So you could define:

Business friction = the cost imposed by distance between business intent and business outcome.

For Town Ruins, this is particularly relevant because the platform itself is supposed to reduce friction between:

tenant ↔ accommodation ↔ landlord ↔ booking ↔ payment

If your internal development organization has excessive friction, you're effectively building a platform designed to reduce external friction while maintaining internal friction.

11. This gives you an interesting two-layer model

Town Ruins has external friction and internal friction.

External

Tenant → platform → landlord

The platform should reduce:

search friction;

communication friction;

booking friction;

payment friction;

information friction.

Internal

Business → administration → development → deployment → operations

Your SDLC should reduce:

requirement friction;

communication friction;

development friction;

deployment friction;

incident-response friction.

So you can think of the entire company as having a friction architecture.

12. The goal isn't “zero friction”

This is where Scott's concept becomes especially useful for SDLC administration.

Some friction is necessary.

For example:

Code review

adds distance between:

Developer → Production

but protects quality.

Staging

adds distance but protects production.

Database constraints

add friction but protect data integrity.

Authentication

adds friction for users but protects accounts.

Approval processes

add friction but can protect business decisions.

Therefore:

Good SDLC administration asks:

Which friction is protective, and which friction is waste?

That's a much better question than:

“How do we make development faster?”

13. Applied directly to Town Ruins

I'd classify your current system roughly like this:

Productive friction

staging environment;

authentication;

database foreign keys;

CI/build checks;

code review;

production separation;

backups;

monitoring;

deployment controls.

These deliberately slow certain actions to reduce risk.

Wasteful friction

unclear ownership;

undocumented dependencies;

duplicated configuration;

inconsistent API contracts;

unclear environment variables;

missing admin endpoints;

frontend/backend assumptions that don't match;

manual investigation required for routine operations;

business requirements that aren't translated into explicit acceptance criteria.

These don't meaningfully protect the business.

They simply increase distance.

14. The ideal Town Ruins SDLC

You ultimately want something like:

Business event

↓
Clearly defined requirement

↓
Traceable technical task

↓
Implementation

↓
Automated validation

↓
Staging

↓
Business acceptance

↓
Controlled deployment

↓
Monitoring

↓
Measured business outcome

The important word is traceable.

At any point you should be able to move backwards:

“Why does this code exist?”

→ Which requirement?

“Why was this requirement created?”

→ Which business problem?

“Did the deployment work?”

→ Which release?

“Did the release produce the desired business result?”

→ Which metric?

That dramatically reduces organizational distance.

The strongest way to apply Scott to Town Ruins

I would formulate the concept for your project like this:

Town Ruins' SDLC can be understood as a system for managing friction of distance between business intent and operational reality. Software architecture, organizational structure, documentation, environments, workflows, and controls either increase or decrease the distance through which information, authority, responsibility, and change must travel. Effective SDLC administration therefore consists not simply of accelerating development, but of making the organization and software sufficiently legible that changes can move safely and predictably from business requirement to production outcome.

That is, in my view, a very strong conceptual framework for your project because it connects Scott's ideas of distance, legibility, administration, and state capacity to practical software governance without forcing the geographic theory onto the technology unnaturally.

That actually makes the friction-of-distance model more useful, because your organization is small enough that the main problem probably isn't bureaucracy in the conventional sense. It's role distance and concentration of decision-making.

If the operation is roughly:

2 developers + 2 CEOs + recruiters

then I'd model it as a very small organization with highly concentrated authority but potentially high communication friction.

1. The organizational map

Something like:

CEOs
↕
Developers
↕
Software / infrastructure
↕
Users / customers

with recruiters operating somewhat peripherally:

Recruiters → talent pipeline → developers

The interesting question isn't "how many management layers are there?"

There are almost none.

The question is:

How far does a business decision have to travel before it becomes an implemented, tested, monitored system change?

With only two developers, that distance can actually become very short—which is an enormous advantage.

2. Your organization has very little structural distance

Suppose CEO A says:

"Password changes need verification and users need an email notification."

In a large company this might travel:

CEO → product manager → security team → architect → engineering manager → developer → QA → DevOps

That's huge organizational friction.

In your operation it could theoretically be:

CEO → Developer → staging → production

That's extremely low friction.

So your organization has the potential to move extremely fast.

The danger is that low distance can also mean low formalization.

3. This is where Scott's "legibility" becomes critical

With only four core decision/technical people, you might think:

"We don't need much documentation. We can just talk."

That works until:

one person is unavailable;

someone forgets why something was implemented;

the two CEOs give different instructions;

developers interpret the same requirement differently;

production has a problem;

a recruiter needs to explain something to a candidate;

a new developer joins;

you need to audit what happened three months later.

Then the organization suddenly develops invisible distance.

The information exists—but only inside people's heads.

That's the organizational equivalent of a territory that exists on paper but isn't legible to the central administration.

4. The two CEOs create a particularly interesting friction point

This may be your biggest organizational risk.

Not because having two CEOs is inherently bad.

Rather:

CEO A → Developer

and

CEO B → Developer

can create two competing administrative channels.

Imagine:

CEO A:

"Prioritize booking."

CEO B:

"Fix account security."

Developer has one available week.

Who decides?

If there isn't an explicit prioritization mechanism, the distance between authority and responsibility becomes ambiguous.

The developer now has to resolve an organizational problem that shouldn't belong to the developer.

That's friction.

5. With two developers, specialization matters enormously

You don't really have the luxury of creating departments.

Instead, you need clear functional ownership.

For example:

Developer 1

application/backend

database

business logic

Developer 2

frontend

infrastructure/deployment

QA/automation

That doesn't mean they can't touch each other's areas.

It means:

Every important system must have a clearly identifiable owner.

Otherwise you get:

"I thought they were handling it."

That's probably one of the most expensive forms of friction in a four-person technical organization.

6. Recruiters are actually part of the SDLC system

If the recruiters are recruiting developers, they're not merely an HR function.

They're affecting the organization's future technical capacity.

You can model the whole thing:

CEOs

→ strategy / capital / priorities

Recruiters

→ talent acquisition

Developers

→ implementation / operation

Platform

→ product

Customers

→ feedback / revenue

So recruitment is actually upstream of your development capacity.

If you need another developer but recruiting takes six weeks to find one, that's organizational friction of distance.

7. Your biggest advantage is that you can keep the map very short

I wouldn't recommend introducing layers just because you're thinking about SDLC administration.

You probably want something closer to:

Business

CEO(s)

↓

Technical execution

Developer 1 ↔ Developer 2

↓

Controlled environments

Development → Staging → Production

↓

Operations

Monitoring → Incident → Business

That's enough.

The administrative system should make this path visible, not add managers to it.

8. I'd introduce only a few formal mechanisms

For an operation of this size, I'd want five things.

1. Single prioritized backlog

Every request goes into one system.

Not:

"CEO A told me on WhatsApp."

Not:

"CEO B mentioned it yesterday."

Everything becomes a traceable task.

2. Explicit priority authority

The two CEOs need a rule for resolving competing priorities.

For example:

Business priority is jointly determined by CEOs.

Developers determine technical implementation, not business priority.

That distinction is extremely important.

3. Technical ownership

Every major subsystem has an owner.

For example:

Dev A
